title: Relational Domain Ontology
Relational Domain Ontology
Relational Domain Ontology
text:
2. Problem
Engineering workflows usually decompose a project into successive representations:
\[
P
\rightarrow
R
\rightarrow
A
\rightarrow
D
\rightarrow
I
\rightarrow
V
\]
where, for example:

\(P\): purpose and mission;
\(R\): requirements;
\(A\): architecture;
\(D\): design;
\(I\): implementation;
\(V\): verification and validation.

Each stage is a transformation:
\[
T_k:X_k\rightarrow X_{k+1}
\]
Conventional project assurance predominantly asks whether the resulting artifact satisfies local criteria:
\[
C_k(X_k)=\text{pass}
\]
However:
\[
\bigwedge_k C_k(X_k)=\text{pass}
\]
does not imply:
\[
X_n \models P
\]
A project may therefore remain procedurally compliant while progressively losing the relations that explain why its components, requirements, and decisions exist.
The proposed name for this phenomenon is:
\[
\boxed{\text{semantic traceability decay}}
\]
More specifically:

loss of relational invariants across lifecycle transformations.

title: Relational Domain Ontology
text:
3. Central Hypothesis
Let:
\[
O_k
\]
represent the accepted relational semantic model at lifecycle instant \(k\), and let:
\[
X_k
\]
represent the current project artifact or workflow state.
The hypothesis is that project coherence can be improved by making the relation:
\[
\mathcal{R}(O_k,X_k)
\]
an explicit engineering observable.
Lifecycle progression is then not judged solely by artifact-local compliance, but by whether relevant semantic relations remain valid, are explicitly revised, or become unresolved.
The intended invariant is therefore not:
\[
O_k=O_0
\]
because the ontology itself may evolve.
Instead:
\[
\boxed{
O_k
\overset{\text{controlled transformation}}{\longrightarrow}
O_{k+1}
}
\]
with explicit evidence for semantic additions, deletions, contradictions, refinements, and propagated consequences.
The objective is semantic continuity under controlled revision, not static ontology preservation.

title: Relational Domain Ontology
Relational Domain Ontology
section: 5. Role of the Relational Domain Ontology
text:
5. Role of the Relational Domain Ontology
The RDO provides persistent semantic relations such as:
derives_from(requirement_r1, intent_i1).

constrained_by(requirement_r1, constraint_c2).

allocated_to(requirement_r1, subsystem_s1).

chosen(architecture_a1).

rejected(alternative_a2).

rejected_because(alternative_a2, constraint_c2).

implements(component_c1, requirement_r1).

verified_by(requirement_r1, evidence_e1).

supports(evidence_e1, claim_c1).
The objective is not the Prolog syntax itself.
The engineering value resides in making relations such as these explicit and queryable.
A lifecycle artifact can therefore be tested for conditions such as:
requirement exists without originating intent
architecture decision has lost its rationale
implementation has no requirement relation
verification evidence supports no defined claim
changed assumption has not propagated downstream
new component violates an architectural constraint
These conditions describe semantic discontinuities rather than merely missing fields.

title: Relational Domain Ontology
text:
6. Compliance Reinterpreted as Feedback
Conventional compliance mechanisms remain useful, but their role is changed.
Instead of:
\[
\text{compliance} \Rightarrow \text{correctness}
\]
the proposal treats compliance observations as signals:
\[
e_k=M(O_k,X_k)
\]
where \(M\) measures a selected consistency property.
Examples:
traceability failure
unsupported claim
missing evidence
unauthorized transition
inconsistent terminology
unpropagated requirement change
architecture/requirement mismatch
These signals qualify the relationship between project state and semantic model.
Conceptually:
semantic model       → reference
project artifact     → observed state
compliance mechanism → sensor
inconsistency        → residual/error
engineering action   → feedback
Compliance is therefore telemetry about alignment, not the semantic authority that defines alignment.

title: Relational Domain Ontology
text:
7. AI Workflow Case
AI workflows provide a strong experimental case because semantic transformation occurs repeatedly:
human intent
    ↓
prompt
    ↓
agent interpretation
    ↓
generated artifact
    ↓
tool invocation
    ↓
second agent
    ↓
summary
    ↓
implementation
Each transformation may preserve syntax while losing semantic relations.
The proposed architecture places the RDO outside the stochastic workflow:
                         RDO
                          │
            ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
            ▼             ▼             ▼
          human         agent A       agent B
            │             │             │
            └──── artifacts/actions ────┘
                          │
                          ▼
                 consistency evaluation
                          │
                          ▼
                       feedback
The agent therefore does not become the authority on project meaning.
Its output is another observable artifact evaluated against the persistent semantic model.

title: Relational Domain Ontology
text:
8. Solver Portfolio
The ontology should remain solver-independent.
Different questions require different formal mechanisms.







Question
Candidate formal method




What relations follow from known relations?
Prolog / Datalog


What complete interpretations satisfy these rules?
ASP / clingo


Is this constraint system satisfiable?
SMT / Z3


Does a counterexample exist?
SMT / theorem proving


Can this state be reached?
Model checking


Is an invariant preserved?
Model checking / formal control


Does a temporal property hold?
Temporal model checking


Which admissible solution minimizes an objective?
Constraint optimization


Are nonlinear real constraints feasible?
nonlinear / δ-SMT


Is a mathematical statement derivable from stated axioms?
theorem proving



This yields the governing relation:
\[
\boxed{
\text{property first}
\rightarrow
\text{formal semantics}
\rightarrow
\text{solver selection}
}
\]
rather than:
\[
\text{choose solver}
\rightarrow
\text{reshape problem around solver}
\]

title: Relational Domain Ontology
Relational Domain Ontology
text:
10. Proposed Demonstrator
A minimal demonstrator should intentionally avoid attempting to model an entire project.
Instead, define one bounded engineering lifecycle containing:
Purpose
   ↓
Requirement
   ↓
Architecture decision
   ↓
Implementation artifact
   ↓
Verification evidence
For example:
Intent I1
    ↓ derives
Requirement R1
    ↓ allocated to
Subsystem S1
    ↓ realized by
Component C1
    ↓ verified through
Evidence E1
Then introduce controlled perturbations.

Perturbation A — orphan requirement
Remove:
\[
derives\_from(R1,I1)
\]
while maintaining every conventional document field.


Perturbation B — rationale loss
Replace an architecture without propagating the original trade-off relation.


Perturbation C — false compliance
Allow all required reviews and tests to report PASS while breaking a semantic relation.


Perturbation D — AI transformation drift
Ask an agent to regenerate an intermediate artifact and observe whether semantic relations survive.


Perturbation E — ontology defect
Introduce an incorrect or inconsistent ontology relation and demonstrate that a solver can still reason correctly relative to the defective model.
This last experiment is particularly important because it demonstrates that:
\[
\text{solver determinism}
\]
cannot replace:
\[
\text{semantic validation}
\]

title: Relational Domain Ontology
text:
11. Evaluation
The demonstrator should compare two workflows.

Baseline
Conventional artifacts, traceability IDs, reviews, compliance checks, and AI prompts.


RDO-backed workflow
The same workflow with explicit relational semantics and consistency evaluation.
Metrics may include:


Semantic relation retention
\[
SRR=
\frac{\text{required semantic relations preserved}}
{\text{required semantic relations defined}}
\]


Orphan relation count
Number of entities without required upstream or downstream semantic relations.


Drift detection latency
Number of lifecycle transformations between introduction of semantic divergence and its detection.


False-compliance rate
Cases where conventional compliance reports success while semantic consistency has already failed.


Reconstruction cost
Amount of external reasoning required to recover why an artifact or decision exists.


AI transformation consistency
Frequency with which generated artifacts preserve required relational constraints across repeated executions.

title: Relational Domain Ontology
text:
12. Expected Demonstration
The intended result is not to prove that relational ontologies eliminate project failure.
The narrower proposition is:

A workflow that explicitly represents and evaluates semantic relations can detect classes of lifecycle drift that conventional artifact-local compliance mechanisms cannot necessarily detect.

A second proposition is:

Different formal reasoning engines can operate over projections of the same semantic model without any particular solver becoming the identity of the engineering architecture.

And a third:

AI stochasticity makes semantic traceability decay easier to observe, but the underlying problem is not specific to AI; it is intrinsic to multi-stage engineering transformations.

title: Relational Domain Ontology
text:
13. Expected Contribution
The proposed contribution is an engineering view in which:
\[
\boxed{
\text{project coherence}
=
\text{controlled preservation and revision of semantic relations}
}
\]
rather than merely:
\[
\text{project coherence}
=
\text{artifact compliance}
\]
The RDO acts as a semantic backbone.
Formal methods provide specialized reasoning over selected properties.
Compliance provides feedback.
Artifacts provide observable projections.
Humans and AI agents perform transformations.
Evidence qualifies the model.
No single representation, solver, agent, or process is promoted to semantic authority.

title: Relational Domain Ontology
What Changes While the Agent Thinks
text:
An assistant asserted a Wi-Fi state that was no longer true, during automation work spanning a phone, a Nitro computer, and a Raspberry Pi. The question underneath it is what the proposed automation actually depended on. Following that upstream moved from Tcl and operating-system commands to hardware, execution time, and external asynchronous events, and reached the assumption beneath the operational claim: an observation collected at one moment was being treated as evidence about a continuously changing runtime.
The research manuscript preserves an edited account of that exchange, including the admissions “I conflated devices and timestamps” and “I confused timestamps with control.” Operational work stopped there, and the investigation turned to time coherence, scheduling, and computational study cases. The central question is: under what conditions can an observation still support an action that takes effect later?
Observation → reasoning → proposed action → eventual effect
             The environment keeps changing throughout.
The resulting Temporal Coherence for Agentic Control manuscript brings together the incident, related literature, saved study results, and twelve complete source files. It keeps their roles visible: an edited conversation records the dispute; publications supply definitions and model assumptions; local programs make selected questions calculable; saved measurements describe a particular execution environment.
The literature review gave the inquiry several distinct perspectives. Age of Information concerns the elapsed time represented by an update. Age of Incorrect Information also considers whether the information remains correct. Work on real-time databases distinguishes the age of individual data from the temporal relationship among several observations. Control research explicitly considers delays between sampling and actuator updates. These connections helped articulate the problem while retaining the assumptions and application boundaries of each source.
Small native programs explored those distinctions. C++ handled calculations, Prolog expressed logical cases, and C recorded scheduling observations. Tcl coordinated the study, while SQL supported queries over its saved results. When Octave failed to start in the recorded Android environment, C++ served as the numerical fallback.
One constructed case made the central issue especially clear. Several observations satisfied the study’s chosen age and timestamp-separation limits. Moving the assumed effect time slightly later caused the age condition to fail, although the separation among the original timestamps stayed unchanged. The observations retained their relationship to one another as they grew older together. A separate illustrative model compared four-second and ten-millisecond observation windows; its transition rates were study inputs, never measured estimates of the project’s network.
The phone experiment supplied a different kind of result. On a Motorola Moto G54 running Android/Termux in ordinary user space, the saved sample recorded:



Requested period
Missed deadlines out of 200 iterations




10 milliseconds
0


1 millisecond
0


100 microseconds
49


10 microseconds
200



Here, a miss meant completion after the probe’s scheduled deadline. The record makes the observed timing behavior tangible, including the unsuccessful cases. It remains one finite phone sample: the manuscript contains no Nitro or Raspberry Pi timing sample, no end-to-end observation-to-effect measurement, and no hard-real-time guarantee. The study produced research artifacts; an operational controller remained undeployed.
The case bears on the foundations of engineering automation: the exchange exposed an assumption that the study could then examine explicitly. What carries into VLSI workflows is the question of how an observation informs a decision and an action taken later. The concrete work is a temporal-reasoning study on one phone; what generalizes is a way to examine what changes between an observation and its effect.
Sources: Recorded incident and research direction; study method and saved results; limitations and bounded conclusions.

title: Approach: investigating the assembly
text:
AI-Pipeline Tools for VLSI Workflows is Group 6’s individual project, developed with AI assistance. This page defines its working approach for the specification and presentation. The central interest is how engineering intent becomes a useful arrangement of concepts, tools, observations, and explanations across a VLSI workflow.
“What is the assembly of it?” asks what makes that arrangement possible. A tool’s visible command is an entrance to its dependencies: the information it receives, the mechanism that processes it, the environment in which it operates, and the assumptions that make its output meaningful. Following those dependencies upstream helps locate the actual problem. In a UART investigation, for example, interpreting a reported mismatch involves the expected transaction, the observed signals, the sampling event, and the meaning of their timestamps.
The Author’s Manifest develops a central distinction within this inquiry: domain meaning and executable organization answer different engineering questions. Understanding a scoreboard involves its relationship to expected and observed behavior; organizing its software involves responsibilities, methods, and communication. Both descriptions matter. The relational domain ontology proposal extends this concern to the relationships connecting purpose, constraints, decisions, and artifacts as work passes through successive representations. Behavior is especially useful here: similar names can conceal different roles, while different entities may exhibit relationships worth comparing.
Prototime names the practice of trying conceptual prototypes and proofs of concept. A small trial gives a question something concrete to encounter: a representation, an observation, an unexpected result, or a limitation. Its value includes discovering that an initial description leaves something out. The next formulation can then become more precise. This gives conceptual inquiry a practical rhythm while allowing independent experiments to retain their own questions.
Native computational tools support that rhythm through mechanisms suited to the task. C++ offers direct structured processing; Tcl expresses coordination; SQLite organizes relations and queries; logic languages express logical conditions. Examining these foundations helps explain why a particular representation or tool belongs in an arrangement. Tool choice follows the operation and the domain relationships it needs to preserve.
AI participation spans implementation, documentation, and learning. The C++ waveform helper joins a concrete programming task with explanatory comments, readable output, and a classroom story. The concept-index case investigates how vocabulary and relationships can become searchable records and graph views. Temporal Coherence examines what may change between an observation and a later action. The Cadence and BIST work brings simulation, synthesis, internal test mechanisms, and engineering documentation into the specification.
These cases give the VLSI main line several concrete contributions while preserving their independent purposes. The present work elaborates their questions, dependencies, proposed specifications, and explanatory examples into a coherent academic presentation.

title: Approach: investigating the assembly
Approach: investigating the assembly
text:
Boundaries
The subject is architectural investigation, specification, elaboration of existing work, and presentation. The existing tools and experiments supply the material the cases examine.
Outside it: FPGA implementation, fabrication, new laboratory campaigns, and deployment. Where a case requires one of these, it is planned separately with its own dependencies and estimate rather than absorbed into the present scope.
Two distinctions hold throughout the text. Appearing together here does not make the contributions part of one implemented pipeline; each retains the purpose it was built for. And existing results, their interpretation, and proposed continuation stay separable, so that a reader can tell which is which.

title: CI-DIGITAL Common Ontology
text:
This document is the project-level, controlled-language specification of the CI-DIGITAL common ontology. It records the vocabulary, relations, and constraints to which descriptions of the project currently commit.
Its entity of interest is the CI-DIGITAL project. It constrains project descriptions; it does not claim that different participants have identical internal representations.
This document is not yet a machine-formal OWL ontology or a SHACL shapes graph. Consequently, the present conformance review is documentary and finite rather than a claim of logical or universal conformance.

title: CI-DIGITAL Common Ontology
text:
This document is the project-level, controlled-language specification of the CI-DIGITAL common ontology. It records the vocabulary, relations, and constraints to which descriptions of the project currently commit.
Its entity of interest is the CI-DIGITAL project. It constrains project descriptions; it does not claim that different participants have identical internal representations.
This document is not yet a machine-formal OWL ontology or a SHACL shapes graph. Consequently, the present conformance review is documentary and finite rather than a claim of logical or universal conformance.

title: CI-DIGITAL Common Ontology
text:
Canonical foundation
The terminology in this section comes from established ontology and architecture-description work rather than from project-specific paraphrase.

Common ontology: a shared representational vocabulary, including relations and constraints, used for consistent exchange among participating agents. Gruber distinguishes consistency with a common ontology from completeness or identity of internal knowledge.
Ontological commitment: the intended interpretation of a vocabulary to which descriptions or participating agents commit. Guarino treats an ontology as a logical theory that constrains admissible models toward intended models.
Interpretation and model: under OWL 2 model-theoretic semantics, an interpretation that satisfies the ontology’s axioms is a model of that ontology.
Architecture viewpoint: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 uses this term for conventions governing the construction, interpretation, and use of architecture views. A viewpoint is distinct from an ontology.
Conformance: SHACL uses a shapes graph to validate a data graph and report whether it conforms. This is distinct from logical satisfaction under OWL semantics.

Let O denote an ontology and I an interpretation. The formal relation used by OWL is:
\[
I \models O
\]
when I satisfies every applicable axiom in O. The set of admissible interpretations is therefore:
\[
\operatorname{Mod}(O)=\{I\mid I\models O\}.
\]
The ontology constrains this set. It does not generally reduce it to one interpretation.

title: CI-DIGITAL Common Ontology
text:
Current ontological commitment
The following statements are the current controlled-language commitments of the project reference. They are not presented as formal OWL axioms:

CI-DIGITAL is the entity of interest of this project ontology.
Content is an established project domain for authored, conceptual, reader-facing, and structured-knowledge material. Storage under content/ can represent this domain but does not establish membership by location alone.
Session has a Domain role relative to Content and a Context role relative to the domains admitted inside Session. These are qualified, Session-specific relations, not universal equivalence between Context and Domain.
Relative to Session, Transcript is an artifact that provides evidence for derived concept lineages. The artifact is not identical to an interpretation derived from it.
Worktree is the accepted current project term for an umbrella of repository-shaped work units. It is explicitly not the Git-worktree concept, and its permanent name remains unresolved.
A filesystem path or file is a representation or storage location. Its name, nesting, or proximity does not by itself establish semantic identity, domain membership, subclassing, or an interface.
A project relation is asserted only when its source and adoption status support it. Otherwise the relation remains unresolved.
Source statements, assistant interpretations, adopted terms, tool observations, and derived conclusions remain distinguishable through conceptual provenance.

text:
Bounded production review
The current review sample is exactly three repository work products. It is evidence about these three products only.
The engineer established the evaluation relation as a comparison between what is expected and what is obtained, followed by the state that should result. In verification terminology:
\[
\Delta = \operatorname{compare}(E,A)
\]
\[
R = \operatorname{resolve}(A,\Delta)
\]
where E is the expected result, A is the actual observed result, \(\Delta\) is the discrepancy, and R is the resulting state. A correct output is not the observation alone or an unexplained pass label. It is the traceable resulting state whose relevant discrepancies with the expectation were resolved or explicitly retained.










Work product
Expected result
Actual observed result
Discrepancy
Resulting state




content/session/ONTOLOGY.md
Session roles are relationally qualified and the file’s scope is distinguishable from the project ontology.
The roles were qualified, but the file did not explicitly classify its representation or point to a project-level reference.
Its local scope could be mistaken for project-wide or machine-formal scope.
The representation status and project-reference link are now explicit; the Session relations remain unchanged.


content/session/content.md
Content is distinguished from the content/ storage representation.
Purpose and provenance, rather than extension or location alone, govern membership.
None within the reviewed criterion.
The work product is retained unchanged as supporting evidence for the common ontology.


content/session/worktree.md
Worktree retains its project meaning without importing Git semantics or claiming a final name.
The meanings are distinguished and the permanent naming branch remains unresolved.
Its observed directory children do not establish formal semantic relations to Hardware or Software.
The work product remains unchanged, and those project-wide relations remain unresolved rather than inferred.



Review result: the three sampled work products now have explicit expectation–observation–discrepancy–result traces. This result does not establish conformance for unsampled artifacts or future descriptions.

title: CI-DIGITAL Common Ontology
text:
Conceptual provenance and corrections

The engineer identified the need for a common reference through which multiple participants could interpret the project structure consistently.
The assistant initially restated exploratory project wording as though it were canonical terminology and generalized Context/Domain duality across six named entities.
The engineer corrected both moves: use terminology grounded in prior research, and do not make a universal claim when a finite production review is the available evidence.
Primary sources established the applicable distinctions: common ontology, ontological commitment, interpretation, model, architecture viewpoint, and conformance.
The assistant consolidated those distinctions into this project-specific controlled-language ontology and withdrew the unsupported universal generalization.
The engineer set the validation boundary to a finite number of production work outputs. The initial number is three, followed by the review recorded above.
The engineer corrected the review criterion: correctness is established through the trace from expected result, through actual observation and discrepancy, to the resulting state. The agent replaced unexplained pass labels with that trace.

The project-specific commitments and their organization are an agent-authored consolidation requested by the engineer. The research terminology retains its external attribution. The finite review does not convert unresolved project relations into adopted commitments.

text:
Formalization boundary
A later machine-readable stage may serialize the adopted vocabulary and axioms as an OWL 2 ontology and express closed data-quality constraints in a separate SHACL shapes graph. That stage has not been performed. It requires stable identifiers and explicit decisions about which project terms denote classes, individuals, or qualified relations.

title: Group 6 Work Plan
text:
Author’s Position — Tackling the Space
I began this project from a refusal: I do not accept a technically plausible conclusion as evidence that the engineering problem was understood. A clean implementation can still be a precise encoding of confusion. Requirements can become specifications, code, reports, and conclusions while the intent that should govern those representations is gradually narrowed, displaced, or merely assumed. My natural response is to “tackle the space”: before selecting a solution, identify the entities, relations, boundaries, assumptions, and evidence that constitute the problem.
In that sense, I think of engineers not as problem-solvers but as problem architects. This is why I treat explanation and teaching as engineering operations rather than presentation afterthoughts. If a conclusion cannot be traced to its purpose, explained clearly, challenged, and corrected, technical polish is not enough. This work therefore investigates whether agentic tools can help preserve that discipline across selected VLSI-workflow transitions while keeping engineering judgment and responsibility explicit.

title: Group 6 Work Plan
text:
2. Object

2.1. Summary
The project will investigate whether agentic tools can help stabilize meaning across transitions in a representative VLSI workflow. Its object is not faster artifact generation or a single automated pipeline. It is an augmented workflow in which original intent, specification, successive engineering representations, and supporting evidence remain traceably related so that semantic drift can be detected, explained, and corrected.
The work begins by asking what constitutes an engineering task: its parts, relationships, behavior, inputs, dependencies, assumptions, and observable results. Existing project material provides the concrete cases. A C++ helper relates a UART verification failure to waveform state. The concept-index work examines how engineering terms and relationships retain their sources. The Cadence study organizes simulation, synthesis, design-for-test, BIST, and boundary-scan questions. An RF direction examines digital control and beamforming requirements. A temporal-coherence study investigates what may change between observing a system and acting on that observation.
One planned object of study within this investigation is the epistemological and ontological organization of knowledge used and produced when agentic tools work alongside representative VLSI workflows. Starting from the repository’s existing conceptual consolidation, the study will identify relevant entities, concepts, relations, contexts, claims, and evidence; establish a controlled vocabulary and taxonomy; record ontological commitments, interpretation rules, conceptual provenance, and epistemic status; and assess alignment with applicable standards, normative references, and established ontology-engineering principles (References 9–16). At selected IC-flow transitions, the meaning expected from recorded intent and specification will be compared with the meaning supported by the resulting artifact and evidence; discrepancies, reviewed corrections, and unresolved limits will be recorded. The trial will evaluate whether this repeated stabilization can reduce, and in bounded cases eliminate, identifiable misunderstanding between transitions. The existing consolidation is preparatory material rather than the completed result; the planned work is to review, correct, extend, and validate it, and to determine whether a machine-readable application ontology and explicit conformance constraints are justified.
AI assistance will be applied primarily to linguistic and semantic work: comparing terminology, relationships, constraints, assumptions, claims, and rationale across representations. Code, scripts, documentation, and diagrams may be produced within the cases, but they are transition artifacts and evidence rather than the central contribution under evaluation. Each case will retain its own purpose and evidence. The final result will report where semantic stabilization succeeded, failed, or remained unresolved without presenting the independent experiments as one already implemented production system.


2.2. General Objective
Develop and empirically evaluate an AI-augmented semantic-assurance method for preserving consistency between original design intent, specification, and successive representations in a representative VLSI workflow, using documented cases to determine whether repeated comparison and reviewed correction can reduce or, within bounded transitions, eliminate identifiable misunderstandings.


2.3. Specific Objectives
The specific objectives are:

O1 — Foundations and scope: establish the project’s purpose, original intent, governing specification, selected transition points, semantic-consistency criteria, and principal architectural questions;
O2 — C++ and UART case: explain how an AI-assisted C++ process connects a UART mismatch to waveform observations and a useful technical account;
O3 — Epistemological and ontological organization: develop and evaluate a controlled vocabulary, taxonomy, ontological commitments, provenance relations, and conformance criteria for interpreting the project’s engineering knowledge;
O4 — Cadence workflow and BIST: describe an AI-assisted Cadence workflow with explicit simulation, synthesis, design-for-test, BIST, and boundary-scan responsibilities;
O5 — RF control and beamforming: define the digital control, interface, synchronization, test, and observation questions for the RF and beamforming direction;
O6 — Temporal behavior: explain how changing state and timing affect the relationship between observation, reasoning, action, and eventual effect; and
O7 — Integration and presentation: consolidate the cases, evaluate their semantic-transition evidence, and produce a coherent repository and academic presentation with traceable claims, readable figures, and consistent references.

title: Group 6 Work Plan
text:
3. Project Relevance

3.1. Research Problem and Justification
VLSI work crosses several technical representations: requirements, architecture, HDL, scripts, simulation results, synthesis reports, test structures, hardware interfaces, and documentation. Each transition interprets engineering meaning in another form. A downstream artifact can be locally valid while omitting, altering, or rebinding part of the intent or specification that should govern it.
The project does not take faster reading, code generation, or document production as its primary result. Its research problem is whether an AI-augmented semantic-assurance loop can detect and correct identifiable interpretation loss across selected IC-flow transitions. The loop compares the meaning expected from recorded intent and specification with the meaning supported by the downstream artifact and evidence, records the discrepancy, subjects a proposed correction to review, and carries the resulting state forward. Requirements traceability and validation (Reference 2), pre- and post-requirements-specification traceability (Reference 14), intent specifications (Reference 15), and semantic interoperability (Reference 16) provide the established engineering concepts. Whether agentic assistance reduces or eliminates misunderstanding remains the empirical question.
The trial applies language models primarily to linguistic and semantic comparison: terminology, relations, claims, constraints, assumptions, and rationale. It does not presume that model output is correct. In this plan, self-correcting means that a reviewed resulting state becomes the comparison basis for the next transition; it does not mean that model output validates itself. A useful result must preserve the evidence for each comparison, the correction applied or rejected, and anything that remains unresolved.
The project is relevant to CI-DIGITAL because it connects digital-circuit subjects to concrete practices of design, verification, test, and technical communication. It is also relevant to engineering education: the selected cases expose both successful results and limitations, allowing the reader to examine how an initial formulation becomes a more precise specification. Existing work provides the basis for this study, so the planned period can concentrate on consolidation, explanation, and bounded continuation rather than claiming a new end-to-end hardware implementation.


3.2. Technological Challenges
The principal challenges are:

preserving original intent, specification meaning, and domain concepts as information moves among people, documents, AI systems, source code, EDA tools, and reports;
distinguishing observed evidence, interpretation, proposal, implementation, execution, and verification;
integrating heterogeneous languages and tools without treating them as one homogeneous pipeline;
making AI-assisted transformations reproducible and attributable;
relating vendor documentation to the exact tool version, interface, library, license, and target technology in use;
defining meaningful stimulus, observation, expected response, and fault scope for BIST and boundary-scan discussions;
identifying interface, clocking, synchronization, calibration, and carrier-compatibility questions in the RF and beamforming direction;
keeping observations temporally valid when the environment can change during reasoning or execution; and
producing a concise academic narrative from contributions that were created for different purposes.

title: Group 6 Work Plan
text:
4. Methodology

4.1. Architecture
The project uses a three-layer semantic-assurance architecture. The first layer establishes the governing intent, current specification, transition boundary, and available evidence. The second observes a selected transition and uses bounded agentic comparison to identify changes in meaning, omissions, contradictions, ambiguity, or unsupported assumptions. The third records the expected meaning, observed meaning, discrepancy, reviewed correction or unresolved state, and resulting semantic state. The resulting state becomes the reference for the next evaluated transition.
This architecture organizes the study; it does not assert that every case executes through a single software platform. Each case may use different tools and representations while following the same requirements for scope, evidence, and explanation.

4.1.1. Engineering Objects and Evidence
Each activity begins with a defined engineering question and the smallest relevant collection of source material. Sources may include requirements, HDL or software, Tcl scripts, logs, waveforms, EDA reports, manuals, papers, structured records, and prior experiment results. Their origin, version, location, and verification state will be preserved where they materially affect the claim.
The UART case begins from a reported mismatch and its waveform context. The concept-index case begins from source records, measured occurrences, and separately reviewed engineering meanings. The Cadence case begins from an inventoried documentation collection and selected DFT, BIST, boundary-scan, and simulation references. The RF case begins from the proposed payload, the FMCOMMS8 interface, the candidate Agilex 5 platform, and the beamforming literature. The temporal case begins from a recorded automation incident, related literature, source programs, and saved measurements.


4.1.2. AI-Assisted Operations and Tools
AI assistance will be used for bounded linguistic and semantic operations whose governing intent, inputs, and expected outputs can be stated. These include source comparison, terminology and binding analysis, traceability across representations, discrepancy formulation, correction proposals, and technical explanation. C or C++, Tcl, SQLite, HDL, and EDA interfaces may produce or inspect evidence within individual cases; those mechanisms do not define the primary AI contribution under evaluation.
An operation is not treated as verified merely because text or code was generated. When execution is required, the environment, command, inputs, outputs, and observed result must be identifiable. When execution is unavailable, the result will remain a specification, proposed continuation, or source-based analysis.


4.1.3. Documentation and Case Integration
Each case will be developed as a readable technical account containing its question, arrangement, evidence, result, limitations, and next engineering decisions. Diagrams and tables will expose relationships that are difficult to communicate linearly. References will stay with the claims they support.
Integration occurs at the level of the project argument: agentic comparison may help preserve intent and specification meaning as work moves between representations. Integration does not erase the independent origin or purpose of the cases. The final presentation will connect their transition evidence while keeping their technical interfaces and completion criteria separate.

7. Action Planning

7.1. Scope Change Management
A proposed scope change must identify the new object, reason, expected output, dependencies, effort, and effect on existing deliverables. It remains a proposal until it is explicitly adopted. New FPGA implementation, fabrication, laboratory campaigns, production deployment, or a unified automation platform will not enter this work plan implicitly through a documentation or research activity.
Changes that affect the academic commitment, schedule, or final deliverables will be reviewed with the advisor. Minor editorial refinements and corrections may be incorporated during the review allocation when they do not alter the project object.


7.2. Execution Mapping and Interdependencies
A1 establishes the original intent, governing specification, selected transitions, consistency criteria, boundaries, and project map used by all later activities. A2 through A6 can then progress independently because each case has its own sources, tools, and acceptance criterion. A7 depends on D1 through D6 because the integrated presentation must evaluate the transition evidence assembled from completed, reviewable case accounts.
Within each case, source availability precedes interpretation, and implementation precedes runtime claims. The Cadence and RF specifications may continue from documentation even when matching licensed tools or hardware are unavailable, but they cannot report simulation, synthesis, BIST insertion, or board validation without identified execution evidence.


7.3. Schedule Change Control
Progress will be reviewed at the end of each monthly activity against the corresponding acceptance criterion. A delay will be recorded with its cause, remaining work, dependency impact, and proposed recovery. Contingency will first absorb corrections within the existing activity. A change that adds a new technical object or exceeds the 84-hour allocation requires a revised estimate and explicit adoption before the schedule is changed.


7.4. Risk Mapping and Action Plan








Risk
Possible effect
Preventive or corrective action




Scope expansion
Independent studies are presented as one implemented pipeline, or the final deliverable becomes too broad.
Maintain case-specific purposes and acceptance criteria; require an explicit scope-change record for new objects.


Insufficient provenance
A generated claim, diagram, or code fragment cannot be traced to its source or operation.
Record material sources, tool or author, version where relevant, and the distinction between observation, interpretation, and proposal.


Unavailable EDA tools, licenses, libraries, or hardware
A specified Cadence, FPGA, RF, or BIST step cannot be executed.
Keep source-based specification distinct from execution; identify the exact missing dependency; use no runtime claim without evidence.


Stale or temporally inconsistent evidence
An observation no longer represents the state on which a later action depends.
Record collection time and relevant state; refresh observations when the environment can change; qualify finite experiment results.


Terminology drift across domains
The same term is used with incompatible meanings, weakening the technical account.
Define terms in their active context; state necessary cross-domain mappings; review terminology during integration.


Schedule pressure
Case work remains incomplete when final integration begins.
Use the monthly acceptance criteria, prioritize the smallest complete case account, and apply contingency before adding scope.


Reference or publication restrictions
Vendor material or project evidence cannot be redistributed in the public deliverable.
Cite permitted sources and describe the relevant finding; keep restricted documents at their authorized location rather than copying them.



The action plan prioritizes a coherent, supportable deliverable over the number of tools, cases, or features mentioned. A narrower claim with identifiable evidence is preferable to a broader claim whose implementation or verification cannot be demonstrated.

title: Concept Index: Giving Every Connection a Source
text:
An engineering project leaves a trail of specifications, source files, verification plans, results and conversations. An index can help someone find a term across that material. A graph can make connections visible. The challenge is deciding what those connections mean.
The CI-DIGITAL concept-index investigation asks how to make recurring language useful for VLSI design, verification and test while retaining its source and context. One practical objective is to follow a concept such as functional coverage back to the definitions, project artifacts and evidence that explain its use.
This gives the question “What is the assembly of it?” a concrete application: inspect what supports a connection and what happened between the original material and the displayed result.

title: Concept Index: Giving Every Connection a Source
text:
What the earlier pilot exposed
The methodology records an earlier “Create Concept Index” pilot built from 18 English interaction records. At its chosen threshold, the sample yielded no repeated contiguous phrases of two to four words. The useful finding was the sample’s limit: a claim about recurring phrases needed more evidence.
Other findings concerned the graph itself. Declared concept assignments appeared alongside measured co-occurrences. Changing a scoring formula raised scores without adding source material. Projecting connections to a domain level reused the same evidence, while concepts without connections disappeared from an edge-based display.
Together, these findings exposed a presentation problem with engineering consequences: a graph can appear richer or more certain without acquiring additional support. The methodology preserves these findings as reported project requirements; its cited original historical exports were unavailable in the repository.

title: Concept Index: Giving Every Connection a Source
section: From visible patterns to explainable meaning
text:
From visible patterns to explainable meaning
The proposed method keeps three kinds of information distinct:

Source material: preserve the source, author or tool, version and location.
Measured patterns: record occurrences and co-occurrences under a stated procedure.
Engineering meaning: create a separate interpretation with a definition, scope, supporting material and review.

For example, finding “coverage” beside “closure” produces an observation. A claim about their engineering relationship needs its own explanation and evidence. A copied passage or a graph projection still leads back to the same underlying source.
The index also allows several perspectives on one concept: the artifact it concerns, the activity it supports, its lifecycle role and its evidence role. A coverage model can belong to several useful views without being forced into one hierarchy. External vocabularies retain their definitions, with explicit mappings where a correspondence is useful.
This case uses an English-language inclusion rule and a VLSI-specific domain boundary. Those choices define the proposed index’s corpus; the wider master’s repository continues to hold independent research and writing. The methodology reserves the word ontology for a later commitment to explicit formal meanings and inference rules.

title: Concept Index: Giving Every Connection a Source
text:
Making selected ideas concrete
The existing local Python/SQLite mock-up represents these distinctions through separate records for sources, observations, candidates and reviewed claims. Its views keep an observation graph distinct from a reviewed semantic graph, retain concepts without edges, and preserve links to the material behind a displayed connection. Versioned records describe changes without overwriting earlier history.
The application described in its README uses local, deterministic processing without an LLM or network service. It remains a mock-up; the README records static authoring checks and leaves runtime acceptance unverified.
Within AI-Pipeline Tools for VLSI Workflows, this contribution addresses the information that a pipeline depends on: terms, meanings, relationships and their origins. Its concrete result is a methodology and a local representation of selected ideas that make the path from source material to a proposed engineering connection inspectable.

title: Evidence-First Methodology for a Governed CI-DIGITAL Concept Index and Typed Concept Graph
text:
The project should build a governed, longitudinal concept index and typed concept graph, not begin with an ontology and not infer one directly from a language model. The system should preserve raw English-language evidence, compute reproducible lexical and temporal observations, and only then allow reviewed semantic assertions. Its central engineering property is traceability: every published term, concept, relation, mapping, score, and status must be recoverable to a versioned source, a transformation record, a review decision, and an intended use.
The method therefore separates six things that are often collapsed:

Corpus evidence: what a person, document, tool, or standard actually contributed.
Deterministic observations: counts, locations, time intervals, and co-occurrences produced by a pinned procedure.
Semantic annotations: proposed meanings, concept boundaries, domains, and relation types.
Verification results: evidence that an artifact or transformation meets specified requirements against a baseline.
Validation results: evidence that the resulting index or graph serves its intended VLSI/IC design, verification, and test uses.
Governance decisions: human approval, publication, deprecation, and retirement.

This separation resolves the principal defects found in the earlier “Create Concept Index” pilot: a sparse 18-record corpus was insufficient for recurring 2–4-gram conclusions; declared concept and domain assignments were mixed with measured co-occurrences; projected domain edges reused concept-edge evidence; formula changes raised scores without adding evidence; declared membership was represented as certainty; edge-derived graphs lost isolated nodes; historical labels could not be authenticated without original exports; and distinct dates were mistaken for distinct sessions.1
The recommended outcome is deliberately modest in formal commitment. A concept or relation is eligible for an immutable release candidate only when its scoped definition or predicate, direction, evidence, counterevidence, review disposition, and intended use satisfy the applicable profile. An independent approval decision may then authorize a distinct publication event that associates the approved claim version with a release. The artifact qualifies as an ontology only if the project later defines formal classes, predicates, constraints, cardinalities, identity/equivalence rules, and inference semantics and then tests their consequences.

title: Evidence-First Methodology for a Governed CI-DIGITAL Concept Index and Typed Concept Graph
section: 1. Research question, purpose, scope, and users
text:
1. Research question, purpose, scope, and users

Research question
How can the project build and govern an evidence-backed index of English lexemes, phrases, concepts, VLSI/IC domains, typed relations, sources, and temporal evolution while preventing provenance contamination, semantic overclaiming, false equivalence, and unsupported semantic claims derived from statistical observations?


Purpose
The method has four purposes:

make recurring language and conceptual structures in CI-DIGITAL inspectable;
improve retrieval across VLSI/IC design, verification, and test artifacts;
create a controlled path from corpus observations to reviewed technical concepts and relations; and
provide assurance records sufficient to explain what was accepted, why, under which version, and for which use.

It is not a method for maximizing graph density. A smaller graph with explicit evidence and stable semantics is preferable to a highly connected graph whose edges cannot be distinguished as observations, annotations, mappings, or logical assertions.


Scope
The primary domain is VLSI/IC design, verification, and test, including relevant artifacts, activities, methods, tools, languages, representations, metrics, lifecycle stages, and evidence. Examples include RTL, netlists, layout, timing, power intent, testbenches, assertions, coverage, formal properties, fault models, scan/test access, verification plans, test results, waivers, nonconformances, and design revisions.
The corpus is English-only at the inclusion boundary. Mixed-language records are segmented before admission; an English segment may be included while an adjacent Portuguese segment remains excluded but addressable in the source registry. Original text is never rewritten or deleted by language selection.


Exclusions
The following are outside the domain corpus unless a future, explicit scope decision introduces a separate scheme:

telecommunications as a research field;
Brazil as a geographic or policy research scope;
construction, BIM, and built-environment vocabularies;
generic software-engineering vocabularies that are not tied to a stated VLSI/IC use;
assistant-generated prose treated as evidence of the corpus owner’s vocabulary;
graph topology treated as evidence of causality, hierarchy, or truth; and
a renderer, publication framework, or site generator. Markdown and future LaTeX/Hugo/Quarto export are supported by neutral identifiers and links, but no renderer is selected here.



Intended users

VLSI/EDA subject-matter reviewers, who decide whether meanings and relations fit authoritative electrical-engineering sources and project use.
Verification and test engineers, who use the index to retrieve requirements, plans, testbench elements, coverage evidence, defects, waivers, and results.
Corpus curators, who acquire, segment, normalize, and version sources without changing their evidential identity.
Data/tool engineers in the interface layer, who implement storage, queries, exports, constraint checks, and reproducible measurements without redefining VLSI concepts.
Assurance reviewers and approvers, who examine claims, counterevidence, procedures, configurations, and release decisions.

title: Evidence-First Methodology for a Governed CI-DIGITAL Concept Index and Typed Concept Graph
text:
2. Repository and pilot evidence

Repository baseline
The repository currently contains a small kb/ source collection and no established documentation, data, or script convention. The user-facing report is therefore placed under docs/research/, while the existing knowledge-base files remain unchanged.








Existing source
Initial routing
Reason




kb/Report_for_NSF_Workshop_on_AI_for_Electronic_Desig.pdf
VLSI/EDA domain corpus
Directly addresses EDA, synthesis, physical design, test, and verification; it also identifies data quality, generalization, robustness, and benchmark infrastructure as material concerns.2


kb/raw/sat18_chronological_backtracking.pdf and kb/raw/2024 - Lazy_Reimplication_in_Chronological_Backtracking.pdf
Conditional VLSI formal-verification subcorpus
SAT/CDCL concepts are admitted only when a source or annotation establishes their role in IC verification, ATPG, equivalence checking, or another scoped VLSI use.


kb/2411.14870v1.pdf
Interface-layer research
The mapping study concerns AI and formal methods across software, systems, and hardware. It can inform evidence methods, but its Computer Science taxonomy must not define VLSI meanings.3


kb/GN99.pdf and kb/GKN04a.pdf
Presentation layer
These graph-visualization papers can inform future displays. Their software-engineering and visualization vocabulary is not evidence for VLSI concept membership.



Routing is a reviewable assertion, not a permanent truth. Each source record must state the decision, reviewer, date, applicable concept scheme, rationale, and superseding decision if reclassified.


Pilot findings as engineering requirements
The prior pilot is a useful fixture but not an empirical map of the complete CI-DIGITAL corpus. Its findings are treated as requirements:







Pilot finding
Method requirement




Eighteen English interaction records yielded no repeated contiguous 2–4-grams at the pilot threshold.
Phrase recurrence is reported as insufficient evidence; zero repeated phrases is a result, not permission to invent phrases. Corpus adequacy gates precede trend claims.


Concept/domain assignments were declared; co-occurrences were measured.
derivation_method distinguishes deterministic observation, rule-based annotation, model suggestion, and human declaration.


Domain edges reused concept-edge evidence.
Projection records derived_from_edge_ids; projected evidence is never counted as independent support.


A formula change increased scores without new records.
Evidence counts and evidence sets are immutable with respect to scoring formulas; a score-version change cannot create an acceptance, approval, or publication event.


Declared membership used confidence=1.0.
Declarations carry an origin and review status, not a probability. No probability is stored without a calibrated predictive interpretation and validation set.


Isolated concepts disappeared from an edge list.
Node inventory is authoritative; graph materialization begins with all in-scope nodes and then adds edges.


Original exports were unavailable.
Historical “exact” or “retrieved exact” status is prohibited unless byte-identical or otherwise authenticated source material is retained.


Different dates were treated as sessions.
distinct_date_count, interaction_group_count, and authenticated_session_count are separate measures. Missing session identity remains unknown.

title: Evidence-First Methodology for a Governed CI-DIGITAL Concept Index and Typed Concept Graph
text:
3. Governing conceptual distinctions

3.1 Lexeme, term, concept, domain, and graph
ISO 704 treats terminology work through relationships among objects, concepts, definitions, and designations, while ISO 1087 supplies the foundational vocabulary for terminology work.45 This methodology operationalizes that distinction as follows:

A lexeme is a language unit observed in a source.
A term occurrence is a lexeme or phrase at a specific source location.
A term record groups variant occurrences without erasing them.
A concept is a reviewed unit of knowledge with a scoped definition and designations.
A domain is a governed subject-field or concept-scheme context. It is not inferred solely from clusters.
A typed concept-graph architecture maintains identified nodes and typed references across distinct named graphs: immutable analytical observations in observation_graph and reviewed semantic claims in reviewed_semantic_graph.
A formal ontology adds declared formal semantics that support defined inferences and consistency questions.

RDF provides a graph data model of subject-predicate-object triples, but using RDF does not make a graph an ontology.6 OWL provides ontology constructs with formally defined meaning, yet an OWL reasoner establishes consequences of asserted axioms rather than whether those axioms correctly describe VLSI practice.7 SKOS is neither a step before RDF nor a step before OWL: it is an RDF vocabulary whose data model is defined as an OWL Full ontology.8


3.2 Frequency, importance, and significance
Three dimensions remain separate:








Dimension
Evidence basis
Permitted conclusion




Lexical recurrence
Token/phrase occurrences under a pinned normalization and segmentation configuration
“This expression recurs in these sources.”


Conceptual importance
Stated retrieval/use requirement, domain authority, risk, or lifecycle role
“This distinction is necessary for this governed use.”


User-specific significance
User-authored recurrence plus explicit review or selection
“This concept is significant to the corpus owner under this criterion.”



The withdrawn ANSI/NISO Z39.19-2005 (R2010) edition separates literary, user, and organizational warrant and ties controlled-vocabulary quality to retrieval purpose, candidate-term review, testing, and maintenance.9 This methodology uses these provisions as historical guidance, not as a current standard, and adapts them as domain-source warrant, corpus-owner warrant, and project-use warrant. A term can be frequent without being important; important without being frequent; or user-significant without being suitable as the preferred VLSI designation.


3.3 Observation, assertion, and truth
An observed co-occurrence states only that two identified items occurred within a declared window. It does not establish:

semantic relatedness;
broader/narrower structure;
part-whole structure;
dependence or enablement;
causation;
validity of either concept; or
truth of the surrounding text.

The observation is still useful: it can nominate a separate candidate record and supply corpus evidence for human review. Review, when successful, produces a separate semantic claim linked to the candidate and qualifying evidence. The observation never changes type or status, and later decisions do not retroactively change what was measured.

title: Evidence-First Methodology for a Governed CI-DIGITAL Concept Index and Typed Concept Graph
text:
4. Conceptual architecture
The architecture is a controlled derivation chain with explicit feedback and release gates:





flowchart TD
    A[Versioned raw sources] --> B[Source registry and immutable identities]
    B --> X[Versioned text extraction, parsing, or OCR with page/span mapping]
    X --> C[Deterministic inclusion, segmentation, and provenance classification]
    C --> D[Reversible normalization and linguistic observations]
    D --> E[Counts, dispersion, temporal measures, and co-occurrence observations]
    E --> F[Candidate terms, concepts, and relation proposals]
    F --> G[VLSI/EDA semantic review with authoritative sources]
    G --> H[Reviewed assertions and mappings]
    H --> I[Structural, logical, semantic, retrieval, and engineering checks]
    I --> J[Independent approval decision]
    J --> P[Publication event for an immutable release]
    P --> K[Use evidence, change requests, deprecation, re-verification, and re-validation]
    K --> B

    L[Interface-layer standards and tools] -. representation/provenance only .-> B
    L -. storage/query/constraint support .-> I
    M[Independent external vocabularies] -. scoped mappings, never silent merge .-> G






This is an architecture description of selected concerns, not the architecture itself. ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 expressly distinguishes an entity’s architecture from an architecture description and does not prescribe a development method, notation, tool, or recording format.10 This methodology uses that distinction to maintain multiple views without pretending that a graph picture describes acquisition, governance, storage, review, query behavior, and release control all at once.
Four named graph/views are mandatory and must not be collapsed into an unlabeled default graph:

provenance_evidence_view: source/artifact versions, acquisition activities, derivation runs, versioned procedures/tools/configurations/environments, segments, evidence items, lineage groups, quotations, mirrors, revisions, and agents.
observation_graph: occurrences, measures, co-occurrences, similarity signals, and projected analytical edges produced by named procedures.
reviewed_semantic_graph: accepted concept definitions, typed semantic assertions, and scoped mappings, each backed by an admissible claim package.
release_governance_view: intended uses, reviews, verification and validation records, approval decisions, publication events, releases, changes, deprecations, and retirements.

The same stable identifier may be referenced across views, but records never change from one view’s record family into another. A new derivation, candidate, claim, decision, or event receives its own identifier and typed link to its inputs. In particular, displaying an observational edge beside a semantic edge does not make their epistemic status equivalent.

Architectural components

Source vault: immutable source payloads or authenticated references, checksums, rights/access notes, and acquisition records.
Execution-provenance registry: acquisition activities; versioned procedures, tools, configurations, and execution environments; generic derivation runs with normalized input/tool/output links; and typed specializations such as extraction/parser/OCR runs with page/span maps and quality uncertainty.
Corpus registry: source identity, scope decision, provenance class, language decision, temporal metadata, and relationships among source, segment, quotation, and derivative.
Observation store: tokens, lemmas, n-grams, spans, frequencies, windows, and co-occurrences with procedure/configuration identifiers.
Semantic workspace: candidate terms, proposed concepts, definitions, domains, typed relations, mappings, counterexamples, and review records.
Published registry: stable identifiers, approved representations, versioned concept schemes, release notes, deprecations, and compatibility mappings.
Assurance ledger: requirements, claims, evidence, checks, results, dispositions, approval, and evidence locations.
Interface/export layer: TSV/JSON/SQLite/Parquet now; RDF/SKOS/OWL/SHACL only when the corresponding semantic commitment and checks are justified.

title: Evidence-First Methodology for a Governed CI-DIGITAL Concept Index and Typed Concept Graph
section: 5. Independent domain corpus and interface-layer policy
text:
5. Independent domain corpus and interface-layer policy

5.1 Namespace and authority separation
The index must maintain at least three independent namespaces:

cid: for governed VLSI/IC design, verification, and test concepts;
ext: for concepts retained in independently versioned external schemes; and
ifc: for representation, provenance, storage, query, formal-semantics, and tooling concepts used by the interface layer.

cid:verification_coverage may be represented using RDF and described with PROV, but rdf:Property, prov:Entity, database “transaction,” or Computer Science “verification” do not thereby become VLSI parent concepts. A relation across namespaces is an explicit mapping with a scope and purpose. It is never a merged glossary entry.


5.2 Source admission policy
A source may be registered because it is operationally relevant to CI-DIGITAL, but every segment and every proposed cid: concept requires its own explicit VLSI-applicability record. Container-level relevance is only a routing hint. A generic database, software-testing, machine-learning, security, telecommunications, geographic-policy, or project-management passage does not enter cid: merely because it appears inside a CI-DIGITAL document.
A segment is eligible for the VLSI domain corpus only when its exact locator and at least one applicable VLSI facet are recorded and one of these bases is documented:

the segment itself defines or constrains a VLSI/IC design, verification, test, manufacturing-test, physical-design, or signoff concept within the cited authority’s scope;
a versioned CI-DIGITAL requirement explicitly assigns the segment a VLSI purpose, artifact, activity, method, concern, or evidence role;
a VLSI subject-matter reviewer identifies the specific VLSI applicability and the qualifying evidence location; or
an external technical source’s exact segment is demonstrably used in a stated VLSI workflow, with the cross-domain conditions recorded.

Authorship by a VLSI body and location inside a VLSI project are not sufficient on their own; only the applicable clause or segment is admitted. If explicit segment-level applicability is absent, the material remains pending, enters ifc: when it describes the interface/tooling implementation, enters an independently versioned ext: scheme when retention is justified, or is excluded. A cid: concept likewise cannot inherit domain membership solely from the source or section that nominated it.
Computer Science methods such as graph algorithms, NLP, databases, formal logic, or provenance may support the system through ifc:. Their terminology remains defined by their own sources. Where a concept is genuinely used in both domains, each definition is retained and a scoped mapping records the correspondence conditions.


5.3 Domain authorities
The IEC’s IEV Part 521 is a primary terminology source for semiconductor devices and integrated circuits.11 IEEE 1800-2023 is the active SystemVerilog design, specification, and verification language standard; IEEE 1800.2-2020 is the active UVM language reference; and IEEE 1500-2022 and IEEE 1838-2019 address embedded-core and 3D-IC test access respectively.12131415 These sources govern only the concepts in their scopes. They do not provide a universal hierarchy for all CI-DIGITAL terms.
Accellera’s UCIS 1.0 is especially instructive: it standardizes coverage-data interoperability and explicitly distinguishes temporal, spatial, and heterogeneous merging; semantically different heterogeneous coverage items should not be automatically merged.16 The index applies the same discipline to concept evidence: storage compatibility is not semantic equivalence.
SEMI’s Compilation of Terms is a candidate locator where manufacturing equipment, materials, process control, traceability, or test interfaces are relevant; a term supplies evidence only when its exact accessible definition/source record and version are captured, and SEMI categories are never imported wholesale into design-verification concepts.17 Si2/OpenAccess and LEF/DEF can anchor design-data representations, while the new Si2 AI-for-EDA ontology can be evaluated as an external, versioned candidate scheme; none is the CI-DIGITAL ontology absent a separate scope decision and admissible claim package.1819

title: Evidence-First Methodology for a Governed CI-DIGITAL Concept Index and Typed Concept Graph
text:
6. Data and provenance model

6.1 Source identity and provenance classes
Every admitted segment must resolve to a source_id and immutable source version. The minimum source and segment model is:







Field
Requirement




source_id
Stable local identifier; never reused.


source_version_id
Identity of the exact payload or reference state used.


source_type
Conversation export, message, uploaded file, repository file, standard, tool output, code artifact, etc.


payload_hash
Cryptographic hash where bytes are available; otherwise null with an access/authentication note.


external_identifier
Conversation ID, DOI, standard number, repository commit, document identifier, or other source-native ID.


origin_actor
User, assistant, external author, tool, system/developer, unknown.


content_role
Dialogue, quotation, code, file text, tool input, tool output, generated summary, metadata.


quoted_source_id
Required when a segment quotes or embeds another retained source.


language_decision
Included-English, excluded-non-English, mixed-segmented, undecidable, pending-review.


scope_decision
cid-eligible VLSI, conditional VLSI, interface layer, external scheme, presentation layer, excluded, pending.


domain_applicability_record_id
Required for cid eligibility; exact segment locator, VLSI facets, basis/evidence, reviewer or rule, status, and version.


span_locator
Byte/character offsets, message ID, page/section, line range, or other reversible locator.


acquisition_activity_id
Required FK to the independent acquisition-activity registry, which resolves its procedure, tool, configuration, environment, actor, time, and log/evidence references.


rights_access_note
Access limits, redistribution limits, and authentication limitations.



W3C PROV distinguishes entities, activities, agents, generation, usage, derivation, attribution, and responsibility, and supports domain-specific specialization.20 The index can map its provenance model to PROV later, but should keep source-native identifiers and richer corpus roles even when no PROV serialization is produced.


6.2 Evidence lineage and independence
Each evidence item may participate in one or more versioned evidence_lineage_group records because different claims can expose different common origins. A named independence_rule defines which lineage relations are collapsed for one claim or analysis. Independence is therefore claim-relative: two items count as independent support only when they were separately originated and neither derives the supported proposition from the other item or from a common underlying item under that rule.
The following rules are binding:

byte-identical mirrors, repository copies, cached copies, and republications belong to the same lineage group;
a quotation, excerpt, translation, generated summary, normalized text, extraction, measurement, or graph projection remains in the lineage of its source, even though it receives a distinct evidence-item identifier;
document revisions and new editions receive distinct source_version_id values but remain in the same lineage group unless a recorded independence analysis establishes a separately originated evidential basis; a changed passage may be new evidence without becoming an independent source;
documents that quote the same standard clause, test report, dataset, benchmark, experiment, or underlying project requirement declare shares_underlying_evidence_with or a more specific dependency and do not multiply independent support for that proposition; and
organizational or author diversity is informative but does not establish independence when the items share the same underlying evidence.

Every counted support set therefore exposes its evidence-item membership, independence_rule_id, candidate lineage groups, collapsed equivalence classes, and unresolved dependencies. Unresolved independence is reported as unknown and is never optimistically counted as independent.


6.3 Provenance separation rules

User and assistant text are separate through every table, measure, and export.
Quoted material is attributed to the quoted source when known and never counted as the quoting actor’s lexical evidence.
Uploaded or repository files contribute to file-author/source statistics, not dialogue statistics.
Code identifiers and comments are separate channels; they are not automatically natural-language terms.
Tool outputs are evidence of a tool run, not user assertions and not external-source originals unless authenticated.
Generated summaries are derivatives; they cannot replace the source payload for verification.
System/developer messages are governance/runtime context and are excluded from user-vocabulary statistics.



6.4 Time and session uncertainty
The temporal model must store the source value and its interpretation separately:







Field
Meaning




timestamp_raw
Exact value received from the source.


timestamp_normalized
ISO 8601 value only when conversion is justified.


time_zone
Source zone, explicit offset, inferred zone, or unknown.


time_precision
Instant, minute, day, month, year, unknown.


time_basis
Source-declared, filesystem metadata, export metadata, inferred, manual.


time_uncertainty_start/end
Interval for uncertain dates.


session_id
Source-authenticated session identifier only.


interaction_group_id
Locally grouped records under a documented grouping rule.



Distinct dates can support distinct_date_count; they do not establish distinct sessions. First-seen and last-seen results inherit the least precise relevant timestamp and must expose uncertainty rather than print a false instant.


6.5 Acquisition and derivation execution identity
Acquisition and derivation are linked but distinct activities. An acquisition_activity obtains or authenticates source material and is referenced by every source_version. A derivation_run transforms one or more registered versioned inputs into one or more registered versioned outputs. Neither is represented by an unvalidated string or an identifier whose target registry is absent.
The execution-provenance spine uses independent immutable registries:

procedures identify logical methods, while procedure_versions identify the exact executable or manual specification used;
tools identify software, services, instruments, or parsers, while tool_versions identify exact releases/builds and integrity locators;
configurations identify configuration families, while configuration_versions hold exact parameter sets and hashes;
execution_environments identify environment families, while environment_versions capture exact runtime, operating-system/container, dependency, locale, and relevant hardware state;
acquisition_activities identify source-obtaining/authentication acts; and
derivation_runs identify transformations and link normalized input, tool, and output association records.

Every derivation run identifies input artifact version IDs + procedure_version_id + tool_version_id(s) + configuration_version_id + environment_version_id + actor/operator + start/end times + log/evidence IDs + output artifact identity/hash, with nullability only where the governing procedure explicitly declares a field not applicable. derivation_run_inputs, derivation_run_tools, and derivation_run_outputs preserve roles and multiplicity. A generic artifact_versions registry gives every source or derived version a valid common FK target; each concrete derived table also carries derivation_run_id, constrained to the run that registered its output.
This record supports reproducibility and change impact. It does not prove semantic correctness. A deterministic procedure can reproducibly generate an incorrect result if its rule or input classification is wrong. Dangling procedure, tool, configuration, environment, acquisition, input, output, or derivation references are release-blocking integrity failures.


6.6 Source bytes to extracted text
PDFs, scans, office documents, HTML, and other non-plain-text sources require an explicit derivation before their text can be segmented. extraction_runs is a one-to-one typed specialization of derivation_runs, not a disconnected execution model. The generic run resolves the input artifact_version_id/source-byte hash, procedure version, parser/OCR tool_version_id values, configuration version, environment version, actor, time, logs, and output artifact identity/hash. The extraction specialization adds mode (embedded_text, parser, OCR, or hybrid), source-page or object to output-span mapping, warnings, extraction-quality measures, and uncertainty or unreadable regions. Page headers, footers, columns, tables, formulas, images, and reading order are not assumed correct merely because text was produced.
Extracted text is a derivative evidence item in the same lineage as its source bytes. Corrections produce a new extraction version linked to the prior result; they do not overwrite source bytes or silently repair quotations. Claims cite the exact extraction version and reversible page/span locator, while high-impact semantic evidence requires inspection of the source rendering when extraction uncertainty could alter meaning.

title: Evidence-First Methodology for a Governed CI-DIGITAL Concept Index and Typed Concept Graph
text:
7. Deterministic extraction and statistical measurement
ISO/IEC/IEEE 15939:2017 organizes measurement around explicit information needs, defined measures, analysis, use, and evaluation of whether results are valid.21 This methodology therefore prohibits “interesting metrics” without a decision they support.

7.1 Required sequence

Resolve acquisition procedure/tool/configuration/environment versions, record the acquisition activity, and register/hash the source artifact version or record why hashing is unavailable.
