title: Temporal Coherence for Agentic Control
text:
Document type: technical evidence paper in Markdown.
Status: research-only; no control application or network configuration is deployed by this paper.
Evidence cutoff: 2026-08-01, America/Sao_Paulo.
Inference policy: technical inference is excluded by instruction.

title: Temporal Coherence for Agentic Control
text:
Abstract
This paper preserves the recorded temporal-control incident from the phone–Nitro–RPi work, records terminology drawn from the cited primary publications and public IEEE standard records, reports the saved analytical and timing observations, and includes the complete study source code.
The incident record preserves the admissions, “I conflated devices and timestamps,” and, later, “I confused timestamps with control.” [12]
Kaul, Yates, and Gruteser define Age of Information as the current monitor time minus the timestamp of the most recently received update. [1, p. 1]
Maatouk, Kriouile, Assaad, and Ephremides define Age of Incorrect Information as a product of a time penalty and an information-error penalty. [2, eq. (3)]
Kao, Lam, Adelberg, Cheng, and Lee distinguish absolute temporal consistency from relative temporal consistency and give separate formulations for continuous and discrete objects. [3, Sec. 4.1]
IEEE 1588-2019 specifies Precision Time Protocol synchronization for clocks in packet-based networked systems. [7]
IEEE 802.1AS-2025 is the active IEEE standard record for timing transport over local area networks; its public description includes synchronized-time transport, timing-source selection, and indication of phase and frequency discontinuities. [8]
The saved Android/Termux timing sample contains four requested periods, 200 iterations per period, and observed miss counts of 0, 0, 49, and 200 for 10 ms, 1 ms, 100 µs, and 10 µs respectively. [16]
Those measurements are one finite user-space sample and are not presented as a worst-case execution-time bound, a schedulability proof, or a hard-real-time guarantee. [22]
Appendix A inventories twelve source files with SHA-256 digests and stated line counts; Appendices B–M contain their complete C, C++, Prolog, Tcl, and SQL listings.
Index Terms— Age of Information, Age of Incorrect Information, temporal consistency, networked control systems, Precision Time Protocol, IEEE 1588, IEEE 802.1AS, event-triggered control, scheduling observation, temporal validity.

title: Temporal Coherence for Agentic Control
text:
I. Evidence Contract

A. Authorized claim classes
This paper uses five claim classes.








Mark
Claim class
Permitted basis




PUB
Published fact
Official IEEE record, published paper, or author-hosted manuscript


REC
Recorded fact
Edited incident record or saved project document


OBS
Observation
Saved measurement row or fresh command result with time and host


COMP
Computed result
Named equation, literal parameters, and reproducible solver output


GAP
Evidence gap
Explicitly unavailable, unmeasured, inaccessible, or undefined evidence



No claim class authorizes a causal conclusion.
No claim class authorizes extrapolation from a finite sample to future executions.
No claim class authorizes a local project rule to be described as an IEEE requirement.
No claim class authorizes a standard’s public summary to be represented as the full normative text.


B. Source hierarchy
Official IEEE Standards Association records are used for standard title, edition status, scope summary, publication status, and publicly exposed terminology. [7]–[11]
Author-hosted or institutional manuscripts are used for paper definitions, equations, theorem premises, and paper-stated limitations. [1]–[6]
The Obsidian engineering-stop note is used only as an edited record of the dialogue, project instructions, and project boundary. [12]
The local study files are used only for code facts, saved results, tool status, and test contracts. [13]–[22]


C. Explicit exclusions
This paper does not infer why the incorrect Wi-Fi statement was produced beyond the admission preserved in the incident record. [12]
This paper does not infer that Age of Information is an actuation-safety proof; source [1] presents it as a status-update timeliness metric.
This paper does not infer that Age of Incorrect Information is a general controller-safety proof; source [2] analyzes a slotted transmitter–receiver estimation model.
This paper does not infer that database temporal consistency is identical to network-interface state validity; source [3] defines consistency for real-time database objects and transactions.
This paper cites the public IEEE descriptions in [7] and [8] only for clock-synchronization and timing-transport scope.
This paper does not infer hard-real-time capability from Android/Termux observations. [16], [22]
This paper does not infer Nitro or RPi timing behavior because neither host contributes a saved timing sample to this study. [13], [22]


D. Version-sensitive terminology
The original source manifest names IEEE 802.1AS-2020. [14]
The current IEEE Standards Association record marks IEEE 802.1AS-2020 as superseded by IEEE 802.1AS-2025. [10]
The current IEEE Standards Association record marks IEEE 802.1AS-2025 as active. [8]
The public 2020 record uses the timing-source phrase “best master.” [10]
The public 2025 record uses the timing-source phrase “best timeTransmitter.” [8]
This paper uses best timeTransmitter when referring to the active 2025 edition and preserves best master only when reporting the historical 2020 wording.

title: Temporal Coherence for Agentic Control
text:
II. Recorded Incident and Stop

A. Status of the incident source
The incident source is the Obsidian note Temporal Coherence - Engineering Stop.md. [12]
That note identifies itself as an edited transcript rather than a verbatim transcript. [12, “Editorial note”]
The note states that the user’s English was corrected while message order, emphasis, tone, technical claims, and intent were preserved. [12, “Editorial note”]
This paper classifies dialogue wording as REC under its claim taxonomy.


B. Recorded sequence
REC-01. The user asked what was being automated. [12, “Terminology and the failed control model”]
REC-02. The assistant answered that network actions, monitoring, and verification were being automated. [12]
REC-03. The assistant stated that this work relied on Tcl, local state, and operating-system commands. [12]
REC-04. The user asked what those terms meant and what they relied on. [12]
REC-05. The assistant described local state as current observed machine facts, Tcl as the language running automation logic, and operating-system commands as depending on the kernel, drivers, services, and hardware. [12]
REC-06. The user asked whether process execution time relied on hardware. [12]
REC-07. The assistant answered yes, through the operating system. [12]
REC-08. The user asked whether external asynchronous events influenced that hardware. [12]
REC-09. The assistant answered yes. [12]
REC-10. The user identified the network as dynamic, asynchronous, and stochastic and challenged the runtime assumption used for it. [12]
REC-11. The assistant responded that state should be continuously revalidated during operations. [12]
REC-12. The user asked how the assistant had made an incorrect assertion about Wi-Fi state. [12]
REC-13. The assistant answered, “I conflated devices and timestamps.” [12]
REC-14. The user asked what timestamps represented. [12]
REC-15. The assistant answered that timestamps represented when each observation was collected. [12]
REC-16. The user distinguished a discrete collected sample from a continuously changing runtime. [12]
REC-17. The assistant answered, “Instant evidence; never current-state certainty.” [12]
REC-18. The user challenged the use of a timestamp as though it were sufficient for work on a continuously changing system. [12]
REC-19. The assistant answered, “I confused timestamps with control.” [12]
REC-20. The user classified the issue as a control-domain foundation problem that compromised user intent. [12]
REC-21. The user then issued “FIRST, STOP” and “YOU ARE GROUNDED.” [12]
REC-22. The assistant answered that it had stopped and would take no further action. [12]


C. Recorded research authorization
The user directed the research to IEEE material on time coherence, scheduling, and applicable equations. [12, “Research authority and boundary”]
The user authorized obtaining papers, writing small study solvers, constructing study cases, performing local calculations, and reporting lessons. [12]
The user did not authorize implementing or deploying an operational solution. [12]
The user assigned Tcl to orchestration and explicitly excluded Tcl from numerical calculation. [12]
The user named Octave, Prolog, C, C++, Fortran, and other compilers as acceptable local study tools. [12]
The user required small, solid solvers and invoked the Unix philosophy. [12]
The user identified Nitro as having an Intel i5 and an NVIDIA RTX 4060 and stated that the effort was no longer smartphone-only. [12]


D. Recorded project requirements
The engineering-stop note records a project requirement that a timestamp identifies an observation time but does not by itself establish current truth, coherence with another sample, or actuation safety. [12, “Binding specifications understood”]
The note records a project requirement to identify the observation target and to avoid merging phone, Nitro, and RPi evidence under the ambiguous word “local.” [12]
The note records a project requirement to distinguish measured facts, computed results, assumptions, inferences, and unverified hypotheses. [12]
The note records a project requirement that a state-dependent operational sequence be owned by a continuously alive local process or controller. [12]
The note records a project requirement for explicit observation, decision, revalidation, action, verification, and deadlines in such a controller. [12]
The note records a project requirement for predetermined non-actuation or abort behavior when required evidence or predicates fail. [12]
These are project requirements recorded in [12]; they are not represented here as normative IEEE requirements.

title: Temporal Coherence for Agentic Control
section: III. Primary Literature and IEEE Standard Records
text:
III. Primary Literature and IEEE Standard Records

A. Age of Information
Kaul, Yates, and Gruteser model a source that generates timestamped status messages, a communication system, and a monitor. [1, p. 1]
If the most recently received update at monitor time (t) carries timestamp (u(t)), the paper defines age as:
\[
\Delta(t)=t-u(t).
\]
[1, p. 1]
The paper defines time-average age over ((0,T)) as:
\[
\Delta_T=\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T\Delta(t)\,dt.
\]
[1, eq. (1)]
The paper states that timely updating is not the same objective as maximizing utilization or minimizing packet-delivery delay. [1, p. 1]
The paper describes queue backlog as one reason that transmitting updates as rapidly as possible can produce delayed status at a monitor. [1, p. 1]
The paper also states that reducing the update rate can leave the monitor with outdated information because updates are absent. [1, p. 1]
Those are statements about the paper’s status-update models; this paper does not extend them to an unstated controller model.


B. Age of Incorrect Information
Maatouk et al. define the conventional age penalty as:
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{age}}(t)=t-U(t),
\]
where (U(t)) is the timestamp of the last successfully received packet at the monitor. [2, eq. (1)]
They define an indicator error penalty as:
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{err}}(t)=\mathbf{1}\{\hat X(t)\neq X(t)\}.
\]
[2, eq. (2)]
They define the general Age of Incorrect Information metric as:
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{AoII}}(t)=f(t)\,g\!\left(X(t),\hat X(t)\right).
\]
[2, eq. (3)]
The paper describes (f(t)) as an increasing time penalty for remaining unaware of the correct status. [2, p. 4]
The paper describes (g(X(t),X(t))) as an information penalty reflecting the difference between the current estimate and the actual process state. [2, p. 4]
For the linear time penalty, it defines:
\[
f_{\mathrm{linear}}(t)=t-V(t),
\]
where (V(t)) is the last instant at which the information penalty was zero. [2, eq. (7)]
For the paper’s selected indicator specialization, it gives:
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{prop}}(t)
=
(t-V(t))\mathbf{1}\{\hat X(t)\neq X(t)\}.
\]
[2, eq. (10)]
The analyzed system is slotted, with time normalized to slot duration. [2, Sec. III-A]
The source process in that model is an (N)-state discrete Markov chain, and the channel realization is modeled as independent and identically distributed Bernoulli behavior over slots. [2, Sec. III-A]
The paper assumes instantaneous ACK/NACK delivery in the model it analyzes. [2, Sec. III-A]
Those are model premises in [2], not local timing observations.


C. Absolute and relative temporal consistency
Kao et al. define temporal consistency for a real-time database as how well maintained data model the actual state of the environment. [3, Sec. 4.1]
They divide temporal consistency into absolute consistency and relative consistency. [3, Sec. 4.1]
For continuous objects, they describe absolute consistency through a maximum-age test against a predefined maximum age (T), also called an absolute validity interval. [3, Sec. 4.1.1]
For a relative-consistent set (R), the paper states:
\[
\forall X,Y\in R,
\quad
\left|\operatorname{timestamp}_X-\operatorname{timestamp}_Y\right|
\le R_{\mathrm{rvi}}.
\]
[3, Sec. 4.1.1]
The paper states that the maximum-age and relative-validity values for continuous objects are based on maximum rates of change and application-transaction correctness requirements. [3, Sec. 4.1.1]
For discrete objects, the paper states that update arrival is sporadic and that a suitable maximum age can be difficult to define because the object changes at an unpredictable rate. [3, Sec. 4.1.2]
For a discrete-object version (x), the paper defines the validity interval:
\[
VI(x)=[LTB(x),UTB(x)],
\]
with the lower bound at the arrival of the update carrying that value and the upper bound at the arrival of the next update. [3, Definition 1]
The paper defines a current version (x_i) by the condition:
\[
t_c\in VI(x_i).
\]
[3, Definition 2]
The paper defines absolute consistency for a discrete item as the availability of a current version at any instant. [3, Definition 3]
For a set (R) of discrete-item versions, the paper defines relative consistency by a nonempty validity-interval intersection:
\[
\bigcap_{x_i\in R}VI(x_i)\neq\varnothing.
\]
[3, Definition 4]
The paper states that a relatively consistent database can remain stale; it gives the example of a database that never installs updates. [3, Sec. 4.2]
The paper distinguishes freshness at transaction read time in a weak absolute-consistent system from freshness at transaction commit time in an absolute-consistent system. [3, Definitions 6 and 7]
These definitions remain database and transaction definitions in this paper.


D. Event-triggered control and execution delay
Tabuada models a plant and feedback law as:
\[
\dot x=f(x,u),
\qquad
u=k(x),
\]
and writes the measurement-error-perturbed closed loop as:
\[
\dot x=f(x,k(x+e)).
\]
[4, eqs. (2.1)–(2.3)]
The paper’s ISS Lyapunov definition requires class-(K) functions satisfying:
\[
\underline{\alpha}(|x|)\le V(x)\le\overline{\alpha}(|x|),
\]
and:
\[
\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}f(x,k(x+e))
\le
-\alpha(|x|)+\gamma(|e|).
\]
[4, Definition 2.1, eqs. (2.4)–(2.5)]
The paper models state sampling at (t_i), computation of (u(t_i)=k(x(t_i))), and actuator update at (t_i+). [4, Sec. 2.2]
It defines () as the time needed to read the sensors, compute the control law, and update the actuators. [4, Sec. 2.2]
Theorem 3.1 states that, if (f), (k), (^{-1}), and () satisfy its stated compact-set Lipschitz conditions and the stated ISS-Lyapunov premise, then for every compact set (S) containing the origin there is an (>0) such that every () admits a (>0) with (t_{i+1}-t_i) for all initial conditions in (S). [4, Theorem 3.1]
The paper explicitly states that the lower-bound guarantee requires sufficiently small (). [4, discussion following Theorem 3.1]
The co-schedulability section assumes a preemptive scheduler in which the control task has highest priority and is executed without delay when the trigger condition is met. [4, Sec. 6]
The paper states that context-switch timing overhead can be represented by enlarging (). [4, Sec. 6]
Its Theorem 6.1 gives a sufficient co-schedulability condition through inflated execution times:
\[
\Delta_i'
=
\Delta_i
+
\left\lceil\frac{\Delta_i}{\tau}\right\rceil\Delta.
\]
[4, Theorem 6.1]
The source identifies this as a sufficient condition under its stated scheduling model. [4, Sec. 6]


E. Networked control and maximum allowable transfer interval
Nešić and Teel analyze networked control systems with a maximum allowable transfer interval, abbreviated MATI, between transmissions. [5]
Their stated conclusion is semi-global practical input-to-state stability under the paper’s conditions and sufficiently small MATI. [5]
The author manuscript’s Lyapunov-UGAS protocol definition bounds a protocol Lyapunov function and requires contraction at transmissions. [5, Definition 1]
For each positive (,c), Theorem 1 requires (^*(,c)) and ({x,w,|e(t_0)|}c), then gives its stated practical error bound. [5, Theorem 1]
Theorem 2 adds its stated no-network ISS premise, retains a sufficiently small (), and gives practical state and network-error bounds under its hypotheses. [5, Theorem 2]
The author manuscript used in [5] describes its MATI conclusion as qualitative and calls for more quantitatively useful formulas that expose degradation as MATI increases.
This paper cites [5] only under its stated transfer-interval conditions.


F. Bounded uncertain time-varying delay
Cloosterman et al. present a discrete-time representation derived from the Jordan form of a continuous-time plant for a networked control system with uncertain time-varying delays. [6, p. 1575, Abstract]
Their abstract states that the represented delays may be smaller or larger than the sampling interval. [6, p. 1575, Abstract]
Their abstract states that the proposed linear-matrix-inequality conditions for stability and feedback stabilization are sufficient conditions. [6, p. 1575, Abstract]
The source record identifies the paper as an IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control technical note, vol. 54, no. 7, pp. 1575–1580, 2009. [6]
No necessary condition or unbounded-delay guarantee is attributed to [6] in this paper.


G. IEEE 1588 clock synchronization
The IEEE Standards Association record identifies IEEE 1588-2019 as active. [7]
The record describes a protocol for precise synchronization of clocks in packet-based networked systems. [7]
The record states that heterogeneous clocks may differ in inherent precision, resolution, and stability. [7]
The record states that profiles provide customization. [7]
The record identifies the protocol as Precision Time Protocol, or PTP. [7]
The record states that PTP supports synchronization to a grandmaster clock. [7]
The record states that corrections for path asymmetry are specified when asymmetry values are known. [7]
This paper cites the public description in [7], not the full standard clauses.
This paper therefore does not invent clause numbers or normative wording for unexposed definitions.


H. IEEE 802.1AS timing transport
The IEEE Standards Association record identifies IEEE 802.1AS-2025 as active and as superseding IEEE 802.1AS-2020. [8]
The public description states that the standard defines protocols, procedures, and managed objects for timing transport over local area networks. [8]
The public description includes synchronized-time transport. [8]
The public description includes timing-source selection, named “best timeTransmitter” in the 2025 record. [8]
The public description includes indication of the occurrence and magnitude of phase and frequency discontinuities. [8]
The IEEE 802 tutorial states that IEEE 802.1AS-2020 includes a profile of IEEE 1588-2019. [9, p. 60]
The tutorial describes mean link delay measurement through the IEEE 1588 peer-to-peer delay mechanism. [9, pp. 62–65]
The tutorial states that delay asymmetry must be measured outside PTP and may be included through managed objects. [9, pp. 62–65]
The tutorial describes offset calculation using receive timestamp, send timestamp, mean link delay, and a known asymmetry correction. [9, pp. 62–65]
In a node that supports multiple domains, the tutorial states that each domain is a separate PTP instance. [9, p. 73]
The tutorial states that the mean link delay for IEEE 802.3 transport depends on physical link characteristics. [9, p. 73]
The tutorial is informative material; it is not represented as the normative standard text.


I. IEEE vocabulary status
The IEEE Standards Association record states that ISO/IEC/IEEE 24765-2017 provides a common vocabulary applicable to all systems and software engineering work. [11]
The IEEE Standards Association record lists P24765 as an Active PAR that supersedes 24765-2017. [11]
This paper cites the public IEEE Standards Association record [11], rather than the full vocabulary-standard text.
No IEEE definition of hard real-time is quoted or relied on in this paper, because the public P24765 record cited here does not expose the draft’s term definitions.
No IEEE definition of deadline is quoted or relied on in this paper for the same reason.
No IEEE definition of runtime is quoted or relied on in this paper for the same reason.
When used for the local study, those terms have the project or study meanings stated in Section IV-B.

title: Temporal Coherence for Agentic Control
text:
IV. Controlled Vocabulary

A. Terms adopted directly from published sources








Term
Controlled meaning in this paper
Source boundary




Age of Information, ((t))
Monitor time minus the timestamp of the most recently received update
[1, p. 1]


Time-average age, (_T)
Integral of age over an observation interval divided by interval length
[1, eq. (1)]


Age of Incorrect Information
Product of time penalty and information penalty
[2, eq. (3)]


Information penalty
Function reflecting the difference between current estimate and actual state
[2, p. 4]


Validity interval
Interval associated with a discrete-object version in the paper’s RTDB model
[3, Definition 1]


Current version
Version whose validity interval contains current time
[3, Definition 2]


Absolute consistency
Source-specific definition; maximum-age rule for continuous objects and current-version availability for discrete objects
[3, Sec. 4.1]


Relative consistency
Source-specific definition; timestamp proximity for continuous sets and interval intersection for discrete versions
[3, Sec. 4.1]

section: V. Local Study Definitions and Equations
text:
V. Local Study Definitions and Equations

A. Effect-time age
The local C++ study defines:
\[
A_{\mathrm{effect}}(u,t_e)=t_e-u,
\]
with rejection when (t_e<u). [17]
This is a local study definition.
It is not attributed to IEEE 1588 or IEEE 802.1AS.
It is not attributed to the control theorem in [4].
Source [1] defines ((t)=t-u(t)); local source [17] separately defines (A_{}(u,t_e)=t_e-u).


B. Snapshot age and skew
For sample timestamps (u_1,,u_n), the local implementation computes:
\[
A_{\mathrm{oldest}}(t_e)
=
t_e-\min_i u_i,
\]
and:
\[
S
=
\max_i u_i-\min_i u_i.
\]
[17]
The implementation accepts the age boundary when:
\[
A_{\mathrm{oldest}}(t_e)\le A_{\max}.
\]
[17]
The implementation accepts the skew boundary when:
\[
S\le S_{\max}.
\]
[17]
Both comparisons are inclusive in the source. [17]
The values (A_{}) and (S_{}) are not derived from plant dynamics in this study. [22]
The saved report notes explicitly leave those engineering parameters undefined. [22]


C. Illustrative two-state continuous-time Markov calculation
The local C++ solver defines the up-to-down transition probability:
\[
P_{\uparrow\rightarrow\downarrow}(D)
=
\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}
\left(1-e^{-(\lambda+\mu)D}\right).
\]
[17]
The implementation rejects negative rates, a negative horizon, and a zero total transition rate. [17], [18]
The rates ( ^{-1}) and ( ^{-1}) are illustrative. [15], [22]
They were not fitted from phone–Nitro–RPi network observations. [22]


D. Local logical admissibility
The Prolog predicate requires a list containing exactly seven facts. [19]
The required facts are:

source(authenticated);
epoch(accepted);
an inclusive nonnegative age bound;
an inclusive nonnegative skew bound;
preconditions(valid);
deadline(feasible);
effect_verification(available).

[19]
This predicate is a local research model.
It is not represented as an IEEE standardized authorization protocol.
It is not represented as a safety case.
It is not deployed. [13]


E. Local timing probe
The C probe uses CLOCK_MONOTONIC for its local timestamps. [20]
It uses clock_nanosleep with TIMER_ABSTIME for absolute release instants. [20]
For each iteration, it defines the deadline as one configured period after the scheduled release. [20]
It advances the next release from the previous scheduled release rather than from the observed finish. [20]
It counts a miss only when finish is strictly later than deadline. [20]
Equality with the deadline is classified as on time by the unit test. [20]
One nanosecond after the deadline is classified as a miss by the unit test. [20]
The loop performs a fixed 32-iteration arithmetic workload between start and finish timestamps. [20]
The probe reports iteration count, miss count, maximum release lateness, and maximum completion tardiness. [20]
On a completed run without a clock-related failure, the probe exits zero when missed==0 and one when missed>0; invalid arguments exit two and clock-related failures exit three. [20]

text:
VIII. Source-Backed Lessons

Lesson 1 — AoI definition and stated status-update scope
Source [1] defines age through (t-u(t)).
Source [1] uses that quantity for status-update timeliness.
The incident record requires a separate project validity basis for present-tense operational claims. [12]


Lesson 2 — Freshness and correctness are separate quantities in the AoII paper
Source [2] states that AoI does not capture the current information content or current monitor knowledge in its remote-estimation setting.
Source [2] multiplies a time penalty by an information-error penalty.
Source [2] gives zero information penalty when the monitor’s estimate matches the process state under its chosen indicator function.
The source model is slotted and Markovian. [2]
No broader controller-safety claim is added.


Lesson 3 — Absolute consistency and relative consistency are not synonyms
Source [3] defines the two terms separately.
For continuous objects, one definition uses maximum age and the other uses timestamp proximity. [3]
For discrete versions, one definition uses current-version availability and the other uses overlap of validity intervals. [3]
Source [3] explicitly gives a relatively consistent yet stale database example.


Lesson 4 — Unpredictable discrete changes are treated differently from continuous-object aging
Source [3] states that a suitable maximum age can be difficult to define for a discrete object whose changes arrive unpredictably.
Source [3] introduces versions and validity intervals for those discrete objects.
The incident record identifies Wi-Fi/link state as the disputed project observation. [12]
This paper does not assert that the database formulation is a network-interface protocol.


Lesson 5 — Control results carry explicit execution-time premises
Source [4] includes () between sampling and actuator update.
Source [4] conditions its inter-execution lower bound on stated regularity assumptions and sufficiently small ().
Source [4] states a specific scheduler model for its co-schedulability result.
Source [4] represents context-switch overhead by enlarging ().
No project action-specific plant dynamics or derived temporal limits are recorded in [22].


Lesson 6 — Networked-control results preserve a transmission-interval condition
Source [5] names MATI as an adjustable transfer-interval parameter.
Source [5] states semi-global practical ISS under its conditions and sufficiently small MATI.
Source [5] retains bounded-set and practical-error parameters in its stated results.
The report notes leave (A_{}) and (S_{}) undefined; they do not provide a MATI value. [22]


Lesson 7 — Cloosterman et al.’s stated bounded-delay and sufficient-condition qualifiers
Source [6] addresses uncertain time-varying network delays under its model.
Source [6] states that delays can be smaller or larger than the sampling interval.
Source [6] calls its LMI conditions sufficient.
No necessary-and-sufficient or unbounded-delay statement is substituted.


Lesson 8 — Clock synchronization and timing transport have stated scopes
Source [7] describes clock synchronization through PTP.
Source [8] describes timing transport, timing-source selection, and timing-impairment indication.
Source [9] describes mean link delay, path asymmetry handling, and separate PTP instances for domains.
The quoted public descriptions in [7]–[9] concern clocks and timing transport; this paper does not cite them as support for application-data correctness.


Lesson 9 — Standard edition status changes
Source [10] now marks IEEE 802.1AS-2020 as superseded.
Source [8] marks IEEE 802.1AS-2025 as active.
The source manifest records IEEE 802.1AS-2020 as the edition in the original study. [14]
This paper separately records the current active edition.


Lesson 10 — Finite observations remain finite observations
The saved TSV has four rows, each with 200 iterations; the report notes characterize it as one finite Android/Termux user-space sample and state that it is not a hard-real-time guarantee. [16], [22]


Lesson 11 — A model-turn sequence was not recorded as a continuous controller
The incident record states that a conversational model turn is not a control loop. [12]
It records the project requirement that changing state be owned by a continuously alive local process or controller. [12]
That requirement remains research-only and undeployed. [12], [13]


Lesson 12 — Device identity is part of the evidence record
The incident record states that phone, Nitro, and RPi observations must not be merged under “local.” [12]
The timing TSV names the Motorola phone as the measured host. [16]
The README records a Nitro SSH timeout rather than a Nitro timing result. [13]
No RPi timing result is saved. [15], [16]

title: Temporal Coherence for Agentic Control
text:
IX. Recorded Improvements and Controls
This section contains only improvements explicitly recorded in the incident note or conditions explicitly stated by sources.
It does not introduce a new architecture.

A. Evidence-language improvements recorded by the project

Name the observed host or process rather than saying only “local.” [12]
Preserve the observation time. [12]
Describe historical observations in the past tense unless continuity is established. [12]
Separate measured facts from computed results. [12]
Separate assumptions from observations. [12]
Separate hypotheses from verified results. [12]
Do not convert a timestamp into an unstated validity interval. [12]
State when the evidence needed for a present-tense claim is unavailable. [12]



B. Runtime improvements recorded by the project

Assign a continuously alive local process or controller to state-dependent operational sequences. [12]
Make observation, decision, revalidation, action, and verification explicit stages. [12]
Attach explicit deadlines to the stages that require them. [12]
Define non-actuation or abort behavior for failed predicates. [12]
Keep the conversational model in a supervisory role rather than representing it as a hard-real-time controller. [12]
Keep phone, Nitro, and RPi as separate clock, scheduler, and failure domains in the evidence record. [12]



C. Study-process improvements recorded by the project

Use Tcl for orchestration rather than numerical calculation. [12]
Use a dedicated numerical language or compiled solver for equations. [12], [13]
Use Prolog for the explicit admissibility conjunction and counterexamples. [12], [19]
Use C monotonic-clock instrumentation for local scheduling observations. [12], [20]
Keep each solver small and responsible for one study problem. [12], [13]
Preserve source identities, URLs, DOI values, and file digests. [12], [14]
Keep research artifacts from becoming deployment policy without a separate approval. [12]



D. Paper-specific citation policy
This paper reports the following source premises when it cites the related results:

Retain the observation-time variable (t) and timestamp function (u(t)) when reporting AoI. [1]
Retain the correctness penalty (g(X(t),X(t))) when reporting AoII. [2]
Distinguish continuous-object maximum age from discrete-object validity intervals. [3]
Retain (), the compact-set Lipschitz conditions on (f), (k), (^{-1}), and (), and the ISS-Lyapunov premise when citing Tabuada’s lower-bound result. [4]
Retain the highest-priority and no-delay scheduler premise when citing Tabuada’s co-schedulability result. [4]
Retain sufficiently small MATI and practical-error qualifiers when citing Nešić and Teel. [5]
Retain “sufficient” when citing Cloosterman et al.’s LMI conditions. [6]
Retain known-asymmetry qualification when citing IEEE 1588 path-asymmetry correction. [7]
Retain the edition number when using IEEE 802.1AS terminology. [8], [10]

title: Temporal Coherence for Agentic Control
text:
X. Corner and Edge Cases

A. Time-ordering cases in the C++ study
EC-01 — Effect before sample. age_at_effect(2.0,1.0) must throw std::invalid_argument. [17], [18]
EC-02 — Empty snapshot. evaluate_snapshot with no sample timestamps must throw std::invalid_argument. [17], [18]
EC-03 — Exact age boundary. Oldest age equal to maximum age passes because the comparison is <=. [17], [18]
EC-04 — Exact skew boundary. Relative skew equal to maximum skew passes because the comparison is <=. [17], [18]
EC-05 — One-picosecond age overrun. The constructed effect time 13.000000000001 produces an expected oldest age of 1.200000000001 and fails the 1.2 limit. [18]
EC-06 — Arrival order. The timestamp vector is intentionally not sorted; minmax_element determines the extrema. [17], [18]
EC-07 — Negative transition rate. The CTMC function rejects a negative rate. [17], [18]
EC-08 — Negative horizon. The CTMC implementation rejects a negative horizon. [17]
EC-09 — Zero total rate. The CTMC implementation rejects failure_rate + recovery_rate == 0. [17], [18]
EC-10 — Zero failure rate. With failure rate zero and recovery rate positive, the expected up-to-down probability is zero. [18]
EC-11 — Zero horizon. With nonnegative rates and horizon zero, the expected transition probability is zero. [18]


B. Logical admissibility cases
EC-12 — Exact seven-fact cardinality. The Prolog predicate first requires list length seven. [19]
EC-13 — Missing deadline fact. Removing the deadline fact causes the expected-failure test to fail admissibility. [19]
EC-14 — Extra fact. Any eighth fact fails the exact-length condition even if the required seven are present. [19]
EC-15 — Nonnumeric age. The predicate requires both age values to satisfy number/1. [19]
EC-16 — Negative age. The predicate requires age and maximum age to be nonnegative. [19]
EC-17 — Nonnumeric skew. The predicate requires both skew values to satisfy number/1. [19]
EC-18 — Negative skew. The predicate requires skew and maximum skew to be nonnegative. [19]
EC-19 — Authentication mismatch. source(unauthenticated) is rejected by the expected-failure test. [19]
EC-20 — Epoch mismatch. epoch(old) is rejected by the expected-failure test. [19]
EC-21 — Invalid preconditions. preconditions(invalid) is rejected by the expected-failure test. [19]
EC-22 — Infeasible deadline. deadline(infeasible) is rejected by the expected-failure test. [19]
EC-23 — Unavailable verification. effect_verification(unavailable) is rejected by the expected-failure test. [19]


C. Timing-probe arithmetic and interface cases
EC-24 — Nanosecond carry. Adding 250000000 ns to 4.900000000 s must produce 5.150000000 s. [20]
EC-25 — Deadline equality. Finish exactly equal to deadline is not after the deadline. [20]
EC-26 — One nanosecond late. Finish one nanosecond after deadline is a miss with tardiness one nanosecond. [20]
EC-27 — Early observation. An observation before its target has zero nonnegative lateness. [20]
EC-28 — Late finish does not move release series. The next release is calculated from scheduled release. [20]
EC-29 — Zero CLI period. Zero is rejected by the positive-integer parser and the CLI test expects exit two. [20], [Appendix I]
EC-30 — Negative CLI period. A leading minus sign is rejected by the parser. [20]
EC-31 — Numeric overflow. strtoull range failure is rejected. [20]
EC-32 — Trailing characters. Input such as 12x is rejected. [20]
EC-33 — Schedule multiplication overflow. The CLI rejects a period/iteration combination that cannot fit its schedule arithmetic. [20], [Appendix I]
EC-34 — Interrupted sleep. clock_nanosleep is retried when it returns EINTR. [20]
EC-35 — Clock failure. Clock and sleep failures return exit three. [20]
EC-36 — Miss classification. A finite probe run may exit zero or one, and the Tcl CLI test requires the exit status to agree with the emitted miss count. [Appendix I]


D. Published-model boundary cases
EC-37 — AoI grows while an estimate can remain correct. Source [2] explicitly identifies this behavior as a limitation of AoI in its estimation model.
EC-38 — Error duration. Source [2] states that its indicator error penalty treats one-slot and hundred-slot error duration with the same instantaneous value.
EC-39 — Discrete object with unpredictable update. Source [3] states that a suitable maximum age can be difficult to assign. [3, Sec. 4.1.2]
EC-40 — Relative consistency with stale data. Source [3] gives a database that never installs updates as a relatively consistent but stale example. [3, Sec. 4.2]
EC-41 — (). Source [4] separately discusses the zero-execution-delay case in its inter-execution analysis. [4, proof of Theorem 3.1]
EC-42 — (>0). Source [4] requires a more detailed argument and sufficiently small (). [4]
EC-43 — Nonpreemptible tasks. Source [4] states that its simple Section 6 strategy relies on preemption and that more elaborate scheduling is needed when that assumption fails. [4, Sec. 7.1]
EC-44 — Transfer-interval condition. Source [5]’s theorem states (^*(,c)).
EC-45 — Delay larger than sampling interval. Source [6] explicitly includes delays smaller and larger than the sampling interval.
EC-46 — Known path asymmetry. Source [7] states correction when asymmetry values are known.
EC-47 — Multiple timing domains. Source [9] states that each domain is a separate PTP instance.
EC-48 — Standard supersession. Terminology copied from IEEE 802.1AS-2020 can differ from the active IEEE 802.1AS-2025 record. [8], [10]

text:
XI. Concerns, Unknowns, and Non-Claims

A. Incident-evidence concerns
The incident note is edited, not verbatim. [12]
It is an edited dialogue record. [12]
None of sources [13]–[22] cited in this paper identifies an exact Wi-Fi command, target, observation time, or response for the disputed assertion. GAP
No causal mechanism beyond the recorded admission is asserted. GAP


B. Clock concerns
The cited analytical and timing TSVs contain no clock-offset field. [15], [16]
The cited analytical and timing TSVs contain no clock-drift field. [15], [16]
The cited analytical and timing TSVs contain no path-asymmetry field. [15], [16]
The cited analytical and timing TSVs contain no mean-link-delay field. [15], [16]


C. Scheduler concerns
The report notes state that the sample had no real-time kernel, task-set admission analysis, worst-case execution-time proof, CPU isolation, or interrupt bound. [22]
The saved maxima are sample maxima only. [16]


D. Network and actuation concerns
No end-to-end observation-to-effect measurement is recorded. [22]
The study README says the programs do not control a target. [13]
No network configuration is changed by the study. [13]
The two cited TSVs have no packet-loss-distribution column. [15], [16]
The two cited TSVs have no delay-distribution column. [15], [16]
No state-transition rates are estimated from the network. [22]
The CTMC rates remain illustrative. [22]


E. Model concerns
The local (A_{}) and (S_{}) values are test literals, not derived action limits. [18], [22]
The Prolog predicate has exactly seven facts because the local source says so, not because an IEEE standard specifies that cardinality. [19]
The local solver exposes two scalar rate inputs (failure_rate, recovery_rate) and one horizon. [17]
The AoII source uses a slotted Markov model with model-specific channel and acknowledgement assumptions. [2]
The temporal-consistency source addresses real-time database objects and transactions. [3]
Source [4] states its plant, feedback-law, ISS-Lyapunov, and regularity premises; report notes [22] state that no project action-specific plant dynamics were supplied.
The networked-control sources retain their own plant, protocol, delay, and stability premises. [5], [6]


F. Terminology concerns
“Fresh” has source-specific meanings in [1]–[3].
“Current” is a formal version property in [3] and a restricted evidence word in the project record [12].
In the cited IEEE public descriptions, synchronization concerns clocks [7] and timing transport [8], [10].
“Coherence” is not asserted as a normative IEEE 1588 or IEEE 802.1AS term in this paper.
This paper does not rely on an IEEE definition of “hard real-time”; it cites only the public P24765 record [11], which does not expose the draft’s term definitions.
“Deterministic” is retained as project wording from [12], not presented as an IEEE-defined property.

XIII. Bounded Conclusions
The incident record contains the assistant admissions quoted in Section II and records a research-only stop. [12]
The primary literature supplies separate formal quantities for age, incorrect information, absolute temporal consistency, relative temporal consistency, execution delay, transfer interval, and bounded time-varying delay. [1]–[6]
The IEEE standard records supply clock-synchronization and LAN timing-transport scope and edition-specific terminology. [7]–[10]
The local study inventory names twelve source files; Appendix A provides their digests and stated line counts. [13], Appendix A.
The report notes state that no action-specific plant dynamics define (A_{}) or (S_{}); timing is one finite Android/Termux sample; no RTX/i5 experiment is included; and no end-to-end I/O or network measurement is included. [22] The cited TSVs contain only the Motorola timing rows and two analytical cases. [15], [16]
No operational controller is implemented or deployed by this evidence paper. [12], [13]

Appendix F. Complete Source — prolog/test_admissibility.pl
:- begin_tests(admissibility).

:- prolog_load_context(directory, TestDirectory),
   directory_file_path(TestDirectory, 'admissibility.pl', Implementation),
   (exists_file(Implementation) -> consult(Implementation) ; true).

call_admissible(Facts) :-
    current_predicate(admissible/1),
    admissible(Facts).

valid_facts([
    source(authenticated),
    epoch(accepted),
    age(1.2, 1.2),
    skew(0.6, 0.6),
    preconditions(valid),
    deadline(feasible),
    effect_verification(available)
]).

test(permits_all_predicates_at_inclusive_boundaries) :-
    valid_facts(Facts),
    call_admissible(Facts).

test(rejects_age_beyond_boundary, [fail]) :-
    valid_facts(Facts),
    select(age(1.2, 1.2), Facts, age(1.200000000001, 1.2), Stale),
    call_admissible(Stale).

test(rejects_incoherent_snapshot, [fail]) :-
    valid_facts(Facts),
    select(skew(0.6, 0.6), Facts, skew(0.7, 0.6), Incoherent),
    call_admissible(Incoherent).

test(rejects_unauthenticated_source, [fail]) :-
    valid_facts(Facts),
    select(source(authenticated), Facts, source(unauthenticated), Changed),
    call_admissible(Changed).

test(rejects_old_epoch, [fail]) :-
    valid_facts(Facts),
    select(epoch(accepted), Facts, epoch(old), Changed),
    call_admissible(Changed).

test(rejects_invalid_preconditions, [fail]) :-
    valid_facts(Facts),
    select(preconditions(valid), Facts, preconditions(invalid), Changed),
    call_admissible(Changed).

test(rejects_infeasible_deadline, [fail]) :-
    valid_facts(Facts),
    select(deadline(feasible), Facts, deadline(infeasible), Changed),
    call_admissible(Changed).

test(rejects_unverifiable_effect, [fail]) :-
    valid_facts(Facts),
    select(
        effect_verification(available),
        Facts,
        effect_verification(unavailable),
        Changed),
    call_admissible(Changed).

test(rejects_missing_required_fact, [fail]) :-
    valid_facts(Facts),
    select(deadline(feasible), Facts, Incomplete),
    call_admissible(Incomplete).

:- end_tests(admissibility).

Appendix I. Complete Source — tests/test_deadline_cli.tcl
#!/usr/bin/env tclsh

proc fail {message} {
    puts stderr "FAIL: $message"
    exit 1
}

proc require {condition message} {
    if {![uplevel 1 [list expr $condition]]} {
        fail $message
    }
}

proc run_capture {command} {
    set stdout_channel [file tempfile stdout_path]
    close $stdout_channel
    set stderr_channel [file tempfile stderr_path]
    close $stderr_channel

    set caught [catch {
        exec {*}$command >$stdout_path 2>$stderr_path
    } result options]

    set stdout_channel [open $stdout_path r]
    set stdout_text [read $stdout_channel]
    close $stdout_channel

    set stderr_channel [open $stderr_path r]
    set stderr_text [read $stderr_channel]
    close $stderr_channel

    file delete $stdout_path $stderr_path

    if {!$caught} {
        set exit_code 0
    } elseif {[dict exists $options -errorcode]
              && [lindex [dict get $options -errorcode] 0] eq "CHILDSTATUS"} {
        set exit_code [lindex [dict get $options -errorcode] 2]
    } else {
        fail "could not execute command: $result"
    }

    return [dict create \
        exit_code $exit_code \
        stdout $stdout_text \
        stderr $stderr_text]
}

if {[llength $argv] != 1} {
    fail "usage: test_deadline_cli.tcl DEADLINE_PROBE"
}

set probe [lindex $argv 0]

set missing [run_capture [list $probe]]
require {[dict get $missing exit_code] == 2} \
    "missing arguments must exit 2"
require {[dict get $missing stdout] eq ""} \
    "invalid input must not emit metrics"
require {[string match "usage:*" [dict get $missing stderr]]} \
    "missing arguments must print usage to stderr"

set zero [run_capture [list $probe 0 3]]
require {[dict get $zero exit_code] == 2} \
    "zero period must exit 2"
require {[dict get $zero stdout] eq ""} \
    "zero period must not emit metrics"

set overflow [run_capture [list $probe 18446744073709551615 2]]
require {[dict get $overflow exit_code] == 2} \
    "overflowing schedule must exit 2"
require {[dict get $overflow stdout] eq ""} \
    "overflowing schedule must not emit metrics"

set finite [run_capture [list $probe 10000000 3]]
set finite_exit [dict get $finite exit_code]
require {$finite_exit == 0 || $finite_exit == 1} \
    "finite run must classify observed misses with exit 0 or 1"
require {[dict get $finite stderr] eq ""} \
    "finite run must not emit diagnostics"

set metrics [string trim [dict get $finite stdout]]
set pattern {^iterations=3 missed=([0-9]+) max_release_lateness_ns=([0-9]+) max_completion_tardiness_ns=([0-9]+)$}
require {[regexp $pattern $metrics -> missed release_lateness tardiness]} \
    "finite run must emit exactly one parseable metrics line"
require {$missed >= 0 && $missed <= 3} \
    "miss count must be within the observed iteration count"
require {($finite_exit == 0 && $missed == 0)
         || ($finite_exit == 1 && $missed > 0)} \
    "exit status must agree with the observed miss count"

puts "PASS deadline CLI"

title: Philosophical affinities: tackling the space
text:
Working map organized around the author’s questions, read alongside the Author’s Manifest, the opening project statement, General Notes, and Domain Theory: Foundations. The latter three records remain in the private source collection. The connections below are proposed reading paths. They do not establish intellectual influence or imply that the author adopts a philosopher’s whole position.
The questions can move between these areas. The map is open to the next encounter.
flowchart LR
    Q["TACKLING THE SPACE"] --- A["Constitution and conditions<br/>Aristotle · Kant"]
    Q --- B["Becoming and coupling<br/>Spinoza · Whitehead · Bergson · Simondon"]
    Q --- C["Trying and intervening<br/>Bacon · Bernard · Hacking · Dewey"]
    Q --- D["Meaning and interpretation<br/>Peirce · Wittgenstein · Cassirer · Gadamer"]
    Q --- E["Evidence and revision<br/>Popper · Feynman · Bachelard"]
    Q --- F["Perspective, practice and history<br/>Nietzsche · Foucault · Merleau-Ponty"]

title: Philosophical affinities: tackling the space
section: What is the assembly of it? What is upstream?
text:
What is the assembly of it? What is upstream?



Thinker
Opening for this inquiry




Aristotle
Distinguish what something consists of, its organization, what produces change, and the purpose involved in its explanation. His account of capacity and actuality also separates what something can do from its present activity. These are philosophical distinctions, not a modern engineering state model.


Immanuel Kant
Investigate the conditions that make experience and judgment possible. This opens a question about the categories already operating when we describe an object. Kant’s necessary conditions of experience differ from freely revisable engineering ontologies.


Gilbert Simondon
Understand technical objects through their development and functioning. His associated milieu brings an object’s dependence on, and participation in organizing, its operating conditions into view. This offers a connection to investigating an assembly beyond its component list.

title: Philosophical affinities: tackling the space
section: What changes, persists, and becomes possible through coupling?
text:
What changes, persists, and becomes possible through coupling?



Thinker
Opening for this inquiry




Heraclitus
An influential interpretation of the river fragment connects persistence with changing constituents. His fragmentary work admits different readings; the useful opening here is the relationship between identity and change. He predates Aristotle.


Baruch Spinoza
The physical discussion following Proposition 13 examines a composite individual through relations among its constituent bodies. Changes in parts can coexist with persistence of an organized relation.


Alfred North Whitehead
Attend to becoming and relations among events. A static description can prompt an inquiry into the process through which the described condition arose. His larger metaphysics carries commitments beyond this engineering analogy.


Henri Bergson
Duration brings continuity and qualitative change into the inquiry. His account of experience invites examination of what an inventory of separated states leaves out. It is not a claim that engineering state models are useless.


Gilles Deleuze, including his collaboration with Félix Guattari
Examine how problems acquire their terms and how concepts are created. This is a proposed connection to the author’s unfinished question about what a problem is and to experiments that change what becomes worth asking.

title: Philosophical affinities: tackling the space
section: What becomes knowable when we try something?
text:
What becomes knowable when we try something?



Thinker
Opening for this inquiry




Francis Bacon
Experiment and comparison contribute to inquiry while habitual judgments, inherited doctrines, and misleading uses of words can obstruct it. His account of induction is a specific historical proposal.


Claude Bernard
An experimental idea guides changes in conditions; results can redirect or contradict the idea. His discussion of counter-tests includes removing a proposed cause. Reading the user’s “Bernard… Bcon” as Claude Bernard and Francis Bacon remains tentative.


Ian Hacking
Experimental arrangements can produce phenomena that become objects of investigation. This gives the coupling question a material dimension: the connection may make something happen. Naming a phenomenon and producing it are different activities.


Charles S. Peirce
Clarify a concept through its conceivable consequences under possible circumstances. This connects a proposed distinction with what difference it could make in an inquiry.


John Dewey
Investigate by developing a difficulty into a question, considering explanations, and varying conditions. His account provides a parallel to exploratory attempts; the author’s term “Prototime” remains their own.

title: Philosophical affinities: tackling the space
section: How does meaning develop through an interface or encounter?
text:
How does meaning develop through an interface or encounter?



Thinker or approach
Opening for this inquiry




Later Ludwig Wittgenstein
Examine what an expression does in its use and how criteria operate in a practice. This meets the manifesto’s example of “interface” carrying different responsibilities in different contexts. Relevant passages include sections 43 and 198–202 of Philosophical Investigations.


Ernst Cassirer
Investigate symbolic forms through which human experience and cultural understanding are organized. Symbols participate in making experience intelligible; different forms have distinct roles.


Hans-Georg Gadamer
Understanding involves interpretation, language, historical circumstances, and dialogue. An encounter can alter expectations that helped make the encounter intelligible.


Phenomenology: Edmund Husserl and Maurice Merleau-Ponty
Attend to lived experience, perception, directed attention, and embodiment. Some of what becomes significant in an encounter is already at work before it is put into words.


Knowing-how: Gilbert Ryle and subsequent debate
Investigate intelligent practical ability and its relationship to propositional knowledge. The relation between knowing how and knowing that remains disputed.


Enactive approaches: Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson, Eleanor Rosch
Investigate cognition through embodied activity and organism–environment relations. This offers a connection to learning through participation; enactivism itself contains distinct approaches.

title: Philosophical affinities: tackling the space
section: What is correctness? What could make an explanation change?
text:
What is correctness? What could make an explanation change?



Thinker
Opening for this inquiry




Karl Popper
Frame conjectures so that experience can challenge them. Tests that a theory survives provide provisional corroboration. This concerns empirical theories; it is not a claim that mathematical proof or formal verification is impossible. Popper’s own account explicitly centers problems and problem-solving.


Richard Feynman
Scientific integrity includes reporting circumstances and alternative explanations that could weaken one’s interpretation. His contribution here is that of a physicist reflecting on experimental practice.


Gaston Bachelard
Familiar representations can become obstacles to scientific understanding. Investigation can demand conceptual reconstruction, including revision of what once seemed obvious.


Georges Canguilhem
Examine norms through relations between living beings and their environments. The proposed engineering connection concerns the grounds of an expectation. His medical and biological subject matter remains distinct from a theory of testbench correctness.

title: Philosophical affinities: tackling the space
section: How did these distinctions become available and authoritative?
text:
How did these distinctions become available and authoritative?



Thinker
Opening for this inquiry




Friedrich Nietzsche
Examine perspectives and valuations involved in interpretation. Bringing perspectives into an inquiry does not make every interpretation equally well supported.


Michel Foucault
Investigate historical practices through which categories, knowledge, and standards become possible and authoritative. This is a historical inquiry into knowledge, practices, and subjects; engineering dependencies are a proposed parallel, not an equivalent concept.

title: Philosophical affinities: tackling the space
section: The cognitive and engineering bridge supplied by domain.pdf
text:
The cognitive and engineering bridge supplied by domain.pdf
The chapter adds approaches to knowing that are not confined to a list of philosophers. It connects cognition, requirements, and the reuse of relational knowledge.







Source discussed in the chapter
Contribution to the map




Dedre Gentner — analogy
A relation can be recognized across different domains. The analogy can also break at consequential differences. Printed pages 86–88.


Eleanor Rosch — categories and prototypes
Categories and representative examples contribute to an account of recognition; the chapter discusses limits when extending this to abstract and functional categories. Printed 86.


Roger Schank — dynamic memory and scripts
Experiences can be organized through recurring sequences of objects, events, actions, and purposes. Printed 87–88.


Michael Jackson — problem frames
Examine dependencies between a designed system and the world it senses and affects. Printed 91–92.


The chapter’s Domain Theory
Model requirements through objects, relations, states, transitions, tasks, and goals. Retain unmatched facts during dialogue and let a proposed model be revised or rejected. Printed 95–100 and 115–124.



These entries are grounded in the supplied chapter Domain Theory: Foundations, whose PDF pages 1–45 correspond to printed pages 85–129. Its reported validation studies and formalization have their own limits; they have not been replicated here.

title: Philosophical affinities: tackling the space
section: Connections that developed through the agents’ exchange
text:
Connections that developed through the agents’ exchange

Simondon with Dewey: changing an arrangement may also change the conditions of investigation.
Spinoza with Wittgenstein: continuing relations and continuing uses of words offer different entrances to calling a transformed arrangement “the same system.”
Bachelard with Bergson and Deleuze: conceptual reconstruction can change the question; continuity of the inquiry itself becomes worth examining.
Hacking with practical knowing: learning to adjust an instrument can change what can be produced and noticed.
Popper with the manifesto’s scoreboard: a test invites examination of the intended relation, the property checked, and the interpretation of its result.
Domain Theory with the author’s second attempt: an analogy can disclose a consequential difference; retaining that difference gives the next attempt something concrete to explore.

These are newly proposed connections from this conversation. They remain available for further exchange alongside The Scholastic Decree.

Selected excerpts in order; this is not a complete transcript.
Author — the contexts present in the passage:

And you should look into thos e 1-13 lines. that revels something impressive: you were in another epistemic domain but was in the same till those 13 lines appear, why? because those lines set a context of Objects, methos, inferace, interaction with mixed domains in itself, because I was talking about objects and methosin the sense of computer programming and interface and interactions as Systems Engineering and its coupling aspects.

and yet, you will keep into them because they are the same thing.


You all were facing the wave of a state transition as it evolve by the time.

Assistant — an interpretation offered in response:

I kept trying to hold the meaning still while you were developing its relations. The same assembly remained in view, with programming structure and system coupling present together. I treated those aspects as separate compartments.

Author:

Probably it will bring no noise and will couple easy

Assistant:

It may couple easily. Here, the shared vocabulary let me continue without noticing the shift you were expressing. That apparent smoothness could itself make the transition harder to perceive.

Author:

And by that it could be settle the question?

Runtime: examining the question that organizes the search

The author first asks whether runtime analysis is a perspective on a cyber system and asks for references and challenge. He then asks what comes before and after runtime. The important progression is between the author’s initial question (bbb21496-23d4-4452-83d3-a82a0a26c39d), his software-engineering correction (bbb2116f-f8f3-4b57-bb3b-7639ccdc8103), and his objection to the inherited premises (bbb21262-deeb-4c49-b106-b1e0b919fb18). section: The voice conversation: why these efforts belong in one account
text:
The voice conversation: why these efforts belong in one account
Source extraction: greeting-dialogue.txt contains the 158 nonempty user/assistant text and voice-transcript records. greeting-ordered.txt additionally retains the historical tool entry containing eight generated Markdown documents and its reported file-generation result.
The discussion begins with the author explaining that he was asked what his AI work has to do with metasurfaces and beamforming. The assistant initially makes the connection mostly through review traceability. The author broadens it:

He uses AI for workflow assistance and tool calls, including the kind of work undertaken around Cadence tools.
Documentation matters because intent can be lost between a project’s conception and its eventual result (7f5654f0-2357-49d8-8ba1-9369752420a0).
His proofs of concept examine gaps at transitions between workflow steps, including what the agent can do and what he needs to inspect locally (243e8245-bfcf-4f2c-8812-4e53d1feb24d).
As a master’s student and aspiring teacher, he wants students to understand a tool’s capabilities and limits. Specifying its operating conditions can itself become a learning activity (132e7add-f81c-4471-ae9d-41d7dac4d500).
He wants help organizing and communicating the relationships so others can inspect the approach and consider using it.

The author explicitly objects when the assistant repeats verification and human responsibility at the expense of other contributions (763abd74-6b2c-4338-a063-050cd060b41b). He then corrects the assistant’s attempt to solve this by simply replacing “multipolar” with “multi-axes.” He asks it to understand and analyze the intent (e9762ec9-b91f-4abe-929e-7f5340335ee9). This matters for our eventual writing: show the different activities through their actual contributions instead of cycling through abstract labels.
The hardware discussion adds another direct account. The author explains his wish to reuse FPGA work across CI-Digital and the master’s project, with Agilex 5 as a candidate platform and a telecommunications application providing a demonstration context. He then clarifies that the PIN-diode metasurface already exists and was handed to him by his adviser; his intended initial contribution is its digital control and test platform (d750099a-c595-4637-9758-033892086863). This is the author’s account of the laboratory situation, not a newly inspected hardware result.
Later, he connects his curiosity about test spaces in digital circuits with possible studies of relations and configurations in metasurfaces (1e01a9f6-ea4a-464b-9cd4-cb54ef3dadbf). He places the extensive simulation and potential physical contribution later. The assistant’s language about structural invariance is an elaboration of that discussion, not a demonstrated cross-domain theorem.
The eight generated documents at assistant message 889ead74-c3d2-4e03-b9f5-7ee26ede68c4 organize workflow, pedagogy, controlled AI use, FPGA control/test, candidate structural correspondences, Agilex, institutional alignment, and an adviser-facing explanation. Their contents were read as derivative drafts. Some early voice replies announce saved Markdown before the later explicit generation record; retain that sequence rather than treating every announcement as a separate created artifact.

title: Dialogue and foundations — reading notes
text:
MANIFEST and the domain chapter
The Author’s Manifest distinguishes the organization of domain meaning from the organization of executable structure. Its scoreboard example makes the distinction concrete: determining what a system evaluates and what its observations mean precedes the choice of classes and methods. The manifest therefore places inquiry into domain meaning before the selection of a structure intended to serve it.
The accompanying dialogue distinguishes the meanings assigned to object, method, interface, and interaction across their respective domains. Earlier notes incorrectly attributed this clarification to a.md; the manifest is the relevant source.
The privately retained external chapter Domain Theory: Foundations examines reusable problem structures, analogy, object collaborations, state transitions, generic tasks, and matching among domain models. Its hire/dispatch and hire/repair examples show why differences in behavior and responsibility can matter more than a set of shared objects. The AIR implementation uses ConceptBase/Telos and Prolog, while the chapter also recognizes the limits imposed by sparse initial descriptions and restricted empirical sorting exercises.
The chapter supplies a comparison framework for the inquiry. It does not establish that the broader phenomenon is captured by its domain families, nor that the concepts under study originated there.

title: Dialogue and foundations — reading notes
text:
Existing foundation drafts
Foundation and purpose, The Scholastic Decree, and Philosophical affinities preserve earlier formulations of the project’s fundamentals, architecture, behavior, experimentation, evidence, and philosophical parallels.
They are useful working history. The latest direct clarifications and the recovered dialogues take precedence where an earlier summary narrows the inquiry, assigns a philosophical origin, or mistakes an assistant formulation for the author’s commitment. The current author describes a potentially recurring phenomenon in behavior whose entities need not stay the same. That remains broader than one two-domain example.

title: Dialogue and foundations — reading notes
text:
Implications for later elaboration
The material supports several concurrent contributions: building small tools, understanding existing tool environments, producing and organizing technical documentation, examining experimental behavior, articulating research questions, and learning through explicit specifications. VLSI workflows provide the main presentation line. Each independent example can show a question, an approach, an artifact, an outcome or open possibility, and what the author learned from it.
These notes prepare that elaboration. They do not prescribe a single architecture for all the efforts.

The historical Jan–Jul records, September 9 analysis tools, derived indexes, acquisition records and analytical evidence have different origins. In this copied archive, even the files called active policy describe the earlier analytical arrangement; their storage does not activate them here.


Method, definitions
A question is translated into a unit, source fields, extraction rules and interpretation. Record volume, authored work and successful outcomes are distinct questions. This is a useful research-method contribution, separate from the historical tool examples.

The additional 713,818 event rows and 50 separate-format messages remain separate. The atlas supplies paths, field coverage and source IDs for later focused reading. Describes recorded activity from January 25 to July 24, 2026 in São Paulo time. Its distinction between stored row time and recorded tool start matters: 66,184 tool records fall on different local days under the two fields. It supplies historical navigation rather than a measure of productivity or AI improvement.


Tooling history
Links 3,677 qualifying creation rows, 12,615 modification rows and 1,972 normalized created paths to stored sessions and later references. Dossiers cover a tree comparator, path-isolation wrapper, command guard, formatting plugin, configuration, mux design and Vivado/UVM Tcl. A matching path does not by itself identify unchanged bytes or a single persistent program.


Catalog intent, catalog report
Describes intended purposes across workflow, agent assets, documentation and VLSI/EDA. The 486 code/build paths, 57 test/fixture paths and 1,429 related assets are files, not 1,972 completed tools. Seventeen examples use inspected source cues; most catalog descriptions use names and first-session context. Its diagrams are placement interpretations, useful for navigation but insufficient to reconstruct an implemented common pipeline.


Work trajectories
Nine deliberately selected sequences show how requests, tools, edits and closing narratives can be read together. Empty-session and multi-topic cases explain why a title cannot substitute for the conversation. These cases are source entrances, not representative sampling.


Friction, seven contextual readings
Distinguishes stored errors, nonzero exits, repeated calls and apparent recovery. The seven readings separate diagnostic questions, scope constraints, design intent, policy changes and interpretation corrections. Useful for examining interactions without reducing all author interventions to failure counts.


Line volumes, definitions
Reports gross recorded volumes: 142,164 generated file-code lines, 549,537 conversational lines and 113,250 completed command/background-launch payload lines. Rewrites, forks and overlapping channels remain included. The contribution is an explicit descriptive measure; these numbers cannot be summed as unique work or relabeled human-authored volume.


Premise findings, repairs
Concrete analytical learning: simulator filelists were mistaken for code, an extensionless Bash file was missed, stored user role was too strong an authorship label, and polished diagrams overstated metadata-derived workflow relations. Repairs preserve quantities where appropriate while correcting meaning. These are defects in the September analysis, not a retrospective verdict on all historical work.

The research report proposes a bounded check grounded in six papers. The later report records discrimination of three already known semantic defects while ordinary totals remained unchanged. This supplies an example of studying one’s analytical procedure; it does not establish autonomous discovery or general validity. No trial was rerun here.

Current analytical utilities index capabilities, provenance and assigned scopes, and check structured interchange/results. Records a bounded local content-shape inspection and its exclusions. It is relevant when selecting excerpts for later presentation; no matched credential values were read or reproduced in this note.
