title: Simulation and language references
text:
Source-reading record for kb/raw/, 10 September 2026. These are external references, not the author’s implementation results. All seven simulation PDFs below were read in full, 49 PDF pages in total, extending the earlier abstract-level inventory. Reading used Poppler text extraction, including visible code, tables, captions and references, with selected visual inspection identified below; it did not execute the examples or reproduce the experiments. Graph curves were not digitized. Historical performance statements retain the conditions and scope of their sources.
Together, these sources offer a specific reading route into mechanisms behind model execution: how processes are scheduled, when they communicate, what parallelism is available, and what changes when real hardware participates. This is relevant to the author’s interest in architecture and behavior. The collection’s presence does not establish that any of these approaches was implemented in his projects.

title: Simulation and language references
text:
Full-reading outcomes

SAGA: independent dataflows rather than one GPU thread per process
Scope: All 6 PDF pages, printed 115–120, including algorithms, experiments and references. Source identity: Vinco, Chatterjee, Bertacco and Fummi, DAC 2012.
SAGA asks how RTL simulation can use a GPU despite heterogeneous processes and frequent synchronization. It builds a process-dependency graph, assumes no circular combinational dependency, and creates independent dataflows. Shared upstream processes may be replicated so that flows can compute locally rather than exchange intermediate values. Each flow receives a serial order; different flows execute concurrently. A separate update kernel transfers next-state values and performs testbench actions.
On a GTX480 and 2.8 GHz Core i7, the paper reports modest gains for individual modules and almost 16× for its assembled embedded platform. The mechanism is more informative than the headline: added computation can save communication, while little parallelism or little computation leaves synchronization prominent. Register demand limits scalability. The claimed equivalence concerns steady-state results under the construction’s assumptions; this is not evidence for unrestricted SystemC semantics. Generated CUDA, datatype translation and scheduling are specific responsibilities of the SAGA/HIFSuite transformation, not benefits supplied merely by compiling C++.


Panda: shared language, distinct modeling responsibilities
Scope: All 6 PDF pages, including model/code examples, scheduler description and references. Source identity: Preeti Ranjan Panda, Synopsys, ISSS 2001; the discussion concerns the then-new SystemC 2.0 beta.
This explanatory paper describes a common C++ library and simulation kernel across system, behavioral and RTL models. It separates refinement of data representation from refinement of communication. A channel’s interface can remain stable while its implementation becomes more detailed. Its examples distinguish a non-suspending method process from a suspendable thread, signal changes from general events, and ordinary interface methods from scheduled SystemC method processes.
The compiler produces a simulator from models, testbench and library; hardware synthesis still requires an appropriate subset. Testbench code need not obey that subset. Reusing a testbench across abstractions is explicitly conditional on careful design. The evaluate/update scheduler can perform several delta cycles without advancing simulated time. These distinctions make the paper useful for understanding what code describes, what schedules it and what may become hardware. It supplies no comparative experiment establishing a universal benefit, and its language/version claims are historical.


Acyclic scheduling: more precise dependencies change execution order
Scope: All 6 PDF pages, including the four-process example, implementation discussion, experiments and references. Source identity: Daniel Gracia Pérez, Gilles Mouchard and Olivier Temam, DATE 2004.
The authors rebuild a restricted cycle-level engine supporting methods, ports and signals. They then reduce repeated process wakeups by adding signal dependencies that reveal order hidden inside a coarse process graph. In the request/acknowledge example, a seemingly cyclic pair of processes can be scheduled with five total wakeups instead of seven. The larger superscalar model needed 68 added dependency declarations in roughly 15,000 lines of source.
The proposed order starts statically; if active signals remain, dynamic scheduling takes over. The authors describe this fallback as accommodating incomplete or incorrect dependency hints. A further lesson comes from the host processor: checking readiness in a generic loop largely erased the gain until the generated scheduler used separate branches and direct calls. Results concern two processor simulators, SystemC 2.0.1 and a 2 GHz Pentium 4. Automatic extraction of dependencies was future work. This is a bounded engine and scheduling study, not a drop-in replacement for every SystemC construct.


Neuromorphic virtual platform: partition boundaries carry time obligations
Scope: All 6 PDF pages, including architecture, segmentation examples, component and workload tables, results and references. Source identity: Melvin Galicia, Farhad Merchant and Rainer Leupers, ISQED 2022, DOI 10.1109/ISQED54688.2022.9806235.
The platform combines RISC-V cores, memory/cache models and memristor-based computing-in-memory accelerators. Each simulation segment retains its own native SystemC kernel. A controller advances segments in parallel and uses channel latency to limit how far one segment’s local time may run ahead before it risks missing another segment’s message.
The experiments compare two uniform segments with four segments arranged around workload. Vector–matrix workloads drawn from named convolutional layers yield reported maxima of 2.3× and 3.3× respectively on the stated 12-core Ryzen host. An underused segment contributes little; increasing the quantum beyond the selected 10,000 instructions can increase waiting for synchronization in memory-heavy execution. Thus partition count alone does not explain speed. The accelerator’s internal controller handles its own micro-instructions; host simulation coordination is a different responsibility. Automatic segmentation is future work, and the study does not establish physical chip performance or timing accuracy for all workloads.


SCPEx: a method request is accepted by its receiving module
Scope: All 10 PDF pages, including primitive semantics, complete visible example listings, M-JPEG case discussion and references. Source identity: Mark Thompson and Andy D. Pimentel, University of Amsterdam. No publication venue or date is established from this supplied copy; it describes an extension over SystemC 2.0.
SCPEx imports Pearl’s message-passing approach into SystemC. Each module has one non-preemptive process and private data. A remote call queues a request; the receiving module chooses when to accept it. A synchronous caller waits for a reply, while an asynchronous caller continues. Calling a method synchronously when it never replies blocks the caller indefinitely. The model must not depend on which ready module the scheduler happens to select first.
The processor/cache/memory example distinguishes computation, a pending synchronous request and idle waiting. In the M-JPEG case, application behavior is separate from an architecture model that accounts for timing consequences. A busy bus’s message queue models contention with first-come-first-served arbitration; a different policy needs an explicit arbiter. Calls and blocking primitives also provide places to collect utilization statistics. More advanced statistics and refinement to mixed/plain SystemC were still being developed. This is a modeling demonstration, not a measured comparison of programming-error rates or simulation speed.


GPU simulation review: mappings must preserve suspension and events
Scope: All 8 PDF pages, printed 132–139, including all four reviewed approaches and 19 references; the reading agent also visually inspected Figures 6 and 7. Source identity: Mahesh Nanjundappa, Anirudh Kaushik, Hiren D. Patel and Sandeep K. Shukla, IEEE HLDVT 2012, DOI 10.1109/HLDVT.2012.6418255.
The paper reviews prior work rather than performing a new common benchmark. Its producer/compute/consumer example shows how communication dependencies constrain parallelism. SCGPSim represents suspendable processes as finite-state segments and maps similar code over different data, using barriers for dependencies. SAGA instead duplicates shared upstream computation to form independent flows. Their different reported results reflect different models, code similarity and communication costs.
A mixed RTL/transaction-level approach places selected processes on CPU or GPU using developer hints. Generated kernels represent suspension state, while wrappers exchange event type, duration and next-state information. This makes responsibility concrete: placement hints, code translation and runtime event exchange perform different jobs. A CUDA/OpenCL comparison also separates compilation, initialization, transfers and execution. Prior speedups quoted by this review are historical claims from distinct studies, not a current ranking or a guarantee for arbitrary models. The other underlying implementations were not independently executed or fully read by reading this review.


Hardware in the loop: coordinate progress by controlling device clocks
Scope: All 7 PDF pages: a publisher cover and article pages 1–6, including the example listing, ten-row results table and four references. The reading agent also visually inspected PDF pages 6–7. Source identity: Hongyun Zheng, Xianghu Wu and Yongchao Tao, Shenzhen Academy of Aerospace Technology; SAMSE 2019, IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering 768 (2020) 072029, DOI 10.1088/1757-899X/768/7/072029. The visible byline takes precedence over unrelated template metadata.
The paper asks how to reuse physical hardware when simulated logical time and device time advance differently. A USB-connected logic chip generates a requested number of clock pulses, acknowledges completion and holds its clock output when no new command arrives. A SystemC thread alternates simulation progress with a pulse request and completion wait. The example uses a one-microsecond cycle and one-millisecond quantum. A separate USB path carries other communication.
Responsibility is distributed across the SystemC module, driver/protocol and clock logic. The listing’s pulse and completion functions are illustrative calls, not a complete driver. Requiring hardware whose relevant progress can be paused is an inference from this mechanism; asynchronous external behavior is not examined. The ten-test table reports “Clock deviation” values from 0 to 2 and “Scale of time, software:hil” values from 980 to 1231, without enough units, normalization or measurement detail to interpret them as precision or speedup. The paper proposes feasibility, not evidence that simulation keeps wall-clock pace or supports arbitrary hardware.

title: Simulation and language references
text:
Connections across the simulation papers
The papers distinguish concurrency in a modeled system from parallel execution on the host. Panda explains the native process and channel roles; SAGA changes the schedule and communication cost; acyclic scheduling exposes dependencies inside processes; and the neuromorphic platform preserves native kernels inside time-bounded segments. These are different ways of using a model’s structure.
SCPEx adds another concrete lesson: hiding queue management does not remove communication semantics. Its queue order selects an arbitration policy, and a synchronous call still needs a reply. This connects with the author’s interest in architecture and behavior through actual execution rules rather than a shared vocabulary alone. None of the sources establishes that every design should use one language, one scheduler or one intermediate representation.
The hardware-in-the-loop scheme adds a physical boundary. Its clock controller coordinates device progress with model progress; it does not merely accelerate code. Across the collection, source code can describe behavior, express a dependency, request a transaction, schedule a simulation or drive a device interface. Identifying which role a piece of code performs is necessary before interpreting its result.

title: Simulation and language references
section: Two terminology sources read in full
text:
Two terminology sources read in full
IEEE1800-DEFINITIONS_ACRONYMS.md is explicitly headed “Context: UVM.” Its definitions describe agents, drivers, monitors, scoreboards, sequences, transactions, and communication roles. Its filename alone does not establish its standard edition. It is useful alongside MANIFEST because it makes the testbench responsibilities concrete.
GLOSSARY_IEEE1800-2023.pdf was read across all three pages, printed pages 1349–1351. The file identifies itself as informative Annex P of IEEE 1800-2023. It distinguishes data objects, types, elaboration, interfaces, processes, assertions, DPI, and VPI.
One useful detail is the glossary’s distinction between a blocking assignment and a blocking statement: the latter is a syntactic classification involving potential suspension, so the shared word does not make them interchangeable. Its assertion discussion also distinguishes obligations, environmental assumptions, coverage observations, and restrictions on formal computation. These concrete differences help explain why reading a term in its native engineering context matters.
The source is a three-page annex, not the complete standard. The surrounding language rules and cited clauses were not all read by reading this excerpt.

text:
Purpose
A four-antenna digital beamformer with AD-FMCOMMS8 and an Agilex 5 board and actuated by a metamaterial deflector.
What a channel represents, where weights are applied, how channel identity is preserved, which synchronization assumptions apply, and what observations support the claimed behavior. Four antennas alone does not specify the number of independent spatial streams or establish a complete MIMO implementation.
Analog Devices’ FMCOMMS8 documentation identifies two ADRV9009 transceivers, four transmit and four receive channels, an FMC HPC connection, and JESD204B data transfer. The exact Agilex carrier’s electrical, clocking, interface, and reference-design compatibility remains an integration question.

title: IC - VLSI Development
section: BIST is a required specification topic
text:
BIST is a required specification topic
BIST makes a fundamental question concrete: what can the design establish about itself, through which internal test mechanism, and within which fault model?








Topic
Verified documentation
Proposed use




Logic BIST
Genus DFT guide, chapter “Inserting Logic Built-In-Self-Test Logic,” beginning at printed page 955.
Explain stimulus generation, response analysis, test control, and the relationship between a fault model and the evidence produced.


Memory BIST
Genus/Modus PMBIST Guide, including architecture, insertion, and verification sections.
Identify how a memory test is specified and what a test result says about the memory being examined.


ADC BIST
Ramp Generator for ADC Built-In-Self Test, a research paper describing a Cadence-based ramp-generator study.
A related mixed-signal example. This is not a Genus/Xcelium manual or evidence that FMCOMMS8 implements that scheme.


Boundary scan
Genus/Modus boundary-scan lab.
Explain test access and interconnection concerns while keeping boundary scan distinct from logic or memory BIST.



For the beamformer mock-up, a candidate self-test story is: define a digital block under test, supply a known internal stimulus, observe a defined response, and record both the result and its limits. The specification must identify the faults it intends to detect and the RF, timing, and calibration questions that require other evidence. Choosing the actual BIST architecture remains design work. Cadence ASIC test insertion does not by itself supply an FPGA or RF-board self-test implementation.

title: Content
text:
Scope
Content includes conceptual works, explanatory documents, and structured knowledge intended to carry meaning for a reader.
It does not automatically include every text file, every directory under content/, or operational governance and control artifacts. Membership follows purpose. A Content artifact may still require a narrower distinction such as source, working material, private material, or public deliverable.

title: Content
text:
Development through interaction

1. Purpose corrected location-based classification
The agent initially treated the Manifest as a project-definition document. The engineer corrected that inference: the Manifest is a personal conceptual critique of recurring problems in how objects are taught and understood, not a document defining the repository (Segments 0842–0845).


2. Function exposed the Content domain
The agent then distinguished conceptual work from README orientation and operational controls. The engineer recognized and named the higher domain as Content (Segments 0846–0856).


3. Content acquired storage expressions
The engineer placed the Manifest and documents under content/, then considered the knowledge base. The agent proposed treating the knowledge base as a distinct child for structured knowledge, and the engineer adopted that placement (Segments 0860–0868).


4. Storage did not become semantic authority
Later, the engineer corrected the use of docs/ as a pre-existing classification for session-derived ideas. The interaction itself supplied the relevant concepts, which had to emerge from its meaning rather than from an existing directory name (Segments 0932–0947).

title: Content
text:
Current formulation

Content is a semantic role for material that carries conceptual, explanatory, or structured knowledge.
The Manifest belongs through its conceptual purpose, not because of its filename or root position.
README orientation and operational controls perform different roles.
Documents and the knowledge base may be represented inside the Content storage domain.
Existing storage categories do not pre-classify newly developed concepts.
Content membership depends on purpose; storage location represents that classification but does not originate it.

title: Domain
text:
Scope
Domain includes a bounded group of relevant entities and relations. Its entities may themselves be symbols, contexts, domains, bindings, semantic relations, or ontologies.
Grouping alone remains an open sufficiency question. A directory name, shared label, or physical location does not independently establish a semantic domain.

title: Domain
text:
Development through interaction

1. Domain began as a practical boundary
The engineer distinguished computer, application, repository, interaction, operational, and Cadence-related domains, correcting terminology that crossed them without justification (Segments 0559–0570).


2. Concept and storage representation separated
The engineer corrected Storage and Development as sibling project domains, then distinguished Development as a concept from development/ as its storage representation. They concern the same object under different contexts without becoming the same relation (Segments 0621–0638).
The engineer also proposed that phases can bound domains and that domains may contain subdomains (Segment 0639).


3. Domain returned to grouped entities
The engineer deliberately reduced Domain to a grouped set of entities, including higher-order entities. A name such as Cadence was insufficient because it could drift without its underlying relations (Segments 0646–0648).
The agent formulated stability as arising from explicit connections rather than the name alone. This is agent wording, not a direct engineer definition (Segment 0658).


4. Domains became inputs to architecture and knowing
The engineer related domains to ontology, interfaces, entity kinds, and bottom-up architectural discovery while leaving top-down abstraction available (Segments 0673–0685).


5. The file tree represented domains compactly
The engineer used the UART path to show that a file tree can activate a denser domain before its contents are read. Later, the engineer rejected docs/ as a session domain merely because the directory existed, requiring the interaction’s meaning to establish the domain (Segments 0870–0946).


6. Concepts became candidate domains
The engineer proposed that a concept with sufficient internal meaning could itself become a domain. The agent supplied the criterion field of possible knowledge, which remains an agent formulation rather than direct engineer wording (Segments 0962–0976).
The engineer later clarified that an actor can participate in several domains simultaneously without merging them, and that an idea can provide a conceptual domain for reasoning.

title: Domain
text:
Current formulation

A domain is a bounded group of relevant entities and relations.
Its members may include higher-order entities such as contexts, domains, bindings, and ontologies.
The same conceptual object may have a storage representation without being reduced to that location.
A path can symbolize and activate a domain without exhausting its meaning.
Concepts can become domains when they establish a bounded field for relevant entities, distinctions, and relations.
One actor may participate in several domains while their meanings remain distinct.
Grouping, boundary, purpose, and relations are all candidate conditions; their exact sufficiency remains open.

title: Domain
text:
Relations








Related concept
Relation
Boundary




Context
Context makes a domain active for present meaning.
Not every Context is proven identical to a Domain.


Ontology
Ontology organizes entity and relation kinds associated with a domain.
Whether it precedes or co-develops with Domain remains open.


Interface and Overlap
Domains may meet through an interface or unresolved overlap.
Neither condition has a complete test.


Storage
A path can represent a domain.
Location alone does not create semantic identity.

title: Epistemology
text:
Scope
Epistemology includes the development and limits of knowing, return to foundations, diagnostic drift, bottom-up and top-down movement, and shared meaning.
It does not provide a complete philosophy of truth, formal epistemic logic, mechanical proof system, or canonical academic theory. External standards were requested as comparison, but their reported applicability is not part of this concept’s internal formation.

title: Epistemology
text:
Development through interaction

1. Knowledge became a process
The engineer described a process of knowledge, knowing, cognition, and learning, and sought outside reference points to compare the developing construction with wider practice (Segments 0659–0667).
The agent named this iterative learning. The label is an agent formulation.


2. Foundation and backtrace became epistemic operations
The engineer described returning to a sound foundation, moving forward when it was sufficiently stable, and repeating the movement when new doubt appeared. Elaboration, research, normalization, and provenance backtrace support that return (Segments 0671–0675).
The immediate criterion was not formal proof. The relation had to make enough sense for inquiry to continue.


3. Drift became evidence of missing understanding
The engineer corrected the agent’s negative treatment of drift. Drift is not failure; it signals an underdefined point where forward movement should pause. Investigating the missing relation can transform unresolved overlap into a more intelligible interface (Segments 0673–0681).


4. Ontology and architecture emerged through inquiry
The engineer said that knowing creates ontology and asked which domains, relations, and entity kinds exist. These distinctions support bottom-up architectural expression while a top-down approach remains available (Segment 0682).
The agent strengthened this into claims about what ontology allows and called it the current best expression. Those formulations remain agent-origin (Segments 0681–0684).


5. Inquiry remained open toward truth
The engineer rejected a final word and described an infinite movement toward truth without complete possession of it. The agent’s phrase “keeping the loop honest” is an interpretation of that orientation (Segments 0685–0686).


6. Shared meaning depended on organized relations
The engineer described reasoning or understanding as organizing relations among symbols from many directions. Normalized semantic relations allow a symbol to carry shared meaning between participants. The strong statement that this understanding is “forever” remains open as literal, experiential, or rhetorical (Segments 0687–0689).
The agent’s “lasting anchor” is a softer interpretation, not engineer wording.


7. Dense meaning became a compression analogy
The engineer compared dense meaning to a ZIP file and asked for academic terminology checking. The agent introduced semantic compression as a candidate technical term, but the interaction did not establish it as the engineer’s wording (Segments 0689–0691).

title: Epistemology
text:
Current formulation

Knowing develops through repeated inquiry rather than one final statement.
Doubt or drift can prompt a return to foundations.
Drift can reveal missing knowledge without constituting failure.
Domains, entity kinds, relations, ontology, and architecture participate in the inquiry.
Bottom-up discovery and top-down abstraction are complementary movements.
Truth remains an unreached horizon in this account.
Shared meaning depends on relations becoming sufficiently normalized between participants.
Dense meaning can be represented compactly, while semantic compression remains an agent-introduced analytic label.

title: Interface and Overlap
text:
Scope
This page concerns crossings among contextual, conceptual, and storage domains. It does not assume that every overlap is an error or that every proposed interface is valid. The interaction did not establish a universal interface test.

title: Interface and Overlap
text:
Development through interaction

1. A missing interface exposed an invalid crossing
The engineer identified that inactive material had been added to the active Storage context without a relation capable of carrying it. The disturbance established a basic condition: contextual crossing requires a relevant relation. — Segments 0611–0614.


2. One object appeared through two contextual views
The engineer distinguished Development as a project concept from development/ as a directory while observing that both concern the same object under different contexts. The agent described the mapping between the conceptual view and the storage representation as an interface. The two-view distinction came from the engineer; the interface label was the agent’s formulation. — Segments 0634–0638.


3. Overlap became a diagnostic condition
The engineer described the poorly understood region between two domains as overlap, not as an already formed interface. Such a region indicates missing understanding and warrants investigation before further propagation. — Segments 0673–0675.


4. Ontology and evaluation entered as unfinished possibilities
The engineer connected ontology with the formation of an interface and introduced the possibility of an evaluator. The agent strengthened this into a proposal: ontology constrains admissible entities and relations, while learning may transform unresolved overlap into a normalized interface. The proposal remains incomplete because no general evaluator or acceptance test was established. — Segments 0675 and 0681.

title: Interface and Overlap
text:
Current formulation

A boundary crossing requires a relevant relation.
An interface makes a cross-domain relation intelligible while preserving distinctions important to each side.
An overlap is a candidate relation that is not yet understood well enough to serve as an interface.
An overlap can reveal missing bindings, knowledge, or ontological alignment.
The same object may have distinct conceptual and storage representations without either containing the other.
Investigation may refine an overlap into an interface, but that outcome is not guaranteed.

title: Concept Lineage Method
text: Concept Lineage Method names the way a recorded conversation becomes a set of concept pages that preserve how meanings formed, were corrected, and were rebound over time. The engineer required that domains emerge bottom-up from the meaning of the interaction rather than from an existing classification, and that each concept be traced as an evolving lineage rather than stated as static fact. title: Concept Lineage Method
text:
Scope
The method concerns preserving the source conversation, discovering concepts from meaning, tracing their states through time, distinguishing contributors and transformations, and representing only justified domain-forming lineages.
It is not a glossary method, keyword count, automatic taxonomy, or license to create a file for every mentioned word. Conceptual elaboration does not itself authorize artifact creation, and a common page frame does not by itself constitute an adopted ontology.

title: Concept Lineage Method
text:
Development through interaction

1. Premature artifact creation exposed the execution boundary
The engineer showed a tree example and asked the agent to explain its understanding, explicitly saying the exchange was elaboration rather than an instruction to execute. The agent acknowledged creating a derived document too early; the engineer allowed it to remain as an example (Segments 0932–0937).
The example did not retroactively turn the preceding discussion into authorization.


2. The existing documentation tree was rejected as the classification source
The engineer stated knowledge of the session’s origin and asked the agent to reread its flow, observe what each meaning was about, and let domains emerge. The agent named this bottom-up domain discovery (Segments 0938–0946).
The meaning of the interaction, not the existing tree, became the classification source.


3. The storage contract was made explicit
The engineer created content/session/ and its transcript/ exception. The engineer required the unedited conversation record under transcript/, no further domain directories, and one Markdown file named for each justified domain directly under session/ (Segments 0947–0954).


4. A Context example was tested
The engineer authorized a small extraction test. The agent created a Context page and described it as only the first major conceptual thread (Segments 0955–0961). The engineer then required later uses, corrections, and rebindings to be traced across the full interaction (Segments 0962–0964).


5. An evolution tree became the accepted model
The agent proposed preserving first appearance, initial meaning, later contexts, drift, corrections, stabilized meaning, and open branches. The engineer said that this captured the requirement and emphasized lineage rather than static fact or truth (Segments 0962–0969).
The components of the list are agent wording. The engineer adopted evolving concept lineage, not necessarily one permanent section order.


6. Concept and domain were related without a final sufficiency test
The engineer stated that a concept can be a domain and asked about the epistemological feasibility of that relation. The agent proposed that a concept becomes domain-forming when it bounds a field of possible knowledge (Segments 0969–0976).
The concept-domain relation is engineer-established. The sufficiency criterion is an agent proposal that was not explicitly adopted before the subject moved on.


7. The scoped instruction became the session ontology
The engineer asked for session-local instructions so the method would persist. After they were written, the engineer identified the instruction as the ontology of the Session domain. The agent explained the relation, and the engineer explicitly adopted it (Segments 0979–0988).


8. The effort became working corpus, not proof of concept
The engineer corrected the agent’s status label: the effort was no longer a POC but the actual working corpus. The agent removed the label (Segments 1003–1009).


9. Whole-session validation was required
The engineer asked that every represented domain be analyzed and corrected against the original exchange that formed its meaning, and warned against drifting over existing drift (Segments 1013–1022).


10. The authorship of the frame remained unanswered
When the engineer asked where the common lineage frame came from, the agent said it came from the conversation and condensed the engineer’s principle that concepts evolve and are rebound. The recorded interaction ends as the engineer asks who creates the lineage (Segments 1023–1026).
No answer was given. Lineage pages therefore preserve composite contribution and cannot be assigned solely to the engineer or to the agent.

title: Knowledge Evolution
text: Knowledge Evolution concerns how an understanding forms, loses alignment, returns to recoverable ground, and continues. The engineer described a process and evolution of knowledge, knowing, cognition, learning, and understanding while the engineer and the agent were grouping domains and relations. Through that interaction, drift became a signal for where inquiry resumes rather than a failure, and the process itself became content worth recording. The title, its separation from Epistemology, and the compact process sketch are agent formulations.

title: Knowledge Evolution
text: Knowledge Evolution concerns how an understanding forms, loses alignment, returns to recoverable ground, and continues. The engineer described a process and evolution of knowledge, knowing, cognition, learning, and understanding while the engineer and the agent were grouping domains and relations. Through that interaction, drift became a signal for where inquiry resumes rather than a failure, and the process itself became content worth recording. The title, its separation from Epistemology, and the compact process sketch are agent formulations.

title: Knowledge Evolution
text:
Scope
Knowledge Evolution concerns the temporal movement through which an understanding is formed, loses alignment, returns to earlier ground, incorporates further distinctions or references, stabilizes enough to continue, and later changes again.
It does not decide which beliefs are true, provide a formal learning algorithm, or certify that the process always succeeds. Those questions belong to epistemic evaluation or later implementation.

title: Knowledge Evolution
text:
Development through interaction

1. Grouping entities opened into a process of knowing
The engineer’s inquiry into domains, bindings, semantic relations, and ontology became what the engineer called the process of knowledge, the evolution of knowing, cognition, and learning (Segments 0646–0665).
The agent called it iterative learning. That compact label is agent wording.
The engineer asked whether an IEEE standard could supply another angle and said that such a perspective could help normalize the discussion with other people. The agent named ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 and 24748-1 as partial parallels (Segments 0659–0666). Those references and their claimed fit are agent statements, not independently verified here.


2. Progress began from recoverable ground
The engineer described backtracing to find a sound foundation and then moving forward. At the next doubt, the same activity resumes: elaborate, research when needed, normalize, and relate the new understanding to the earlier foundation through provenance (Segments 0671–0675).


3. Drift determined where learning resumed
The engineer explicitly rebound drift from failure to signal. An underdefined point stops forward movement; resolving the missing knowledge can establish a usable interface and allow the inquiry to grow and continue (Segments 0673–0681).


4. Movement occurred upward and downward
The engineer described bottom-up work from entity kinds and relations toward domains and architecture, also named a top-down approach, and said that abstraction through many levels is difficult (Segment 0682).
The agent’s sequence from entities to domains to abstractions and then testing downward is an agent reconstruction, not the engineer’s stated procedure (Segment 0684).


5. The process stayed open and produced shared symbols
The engineer rejected a final endpoint, then described understanding as organizing relations among symbols until a shared meaning becomes available, using a ZIP-file comparison for the density of that meaning (Segments 0685–0689).


6. The process itself became requested content
The engineer asked that the exchange be recorded because the evolution of Development, knowing, knowledge, and understanding would be an important part of the work (Segments 0694–0718). The engineer required the factual record to remain complete and any reconstruction or analysis to remain separate from it.


7. Communication supplied a later shared-meaning use
During the file-tree discussion, the engineer said that communication is not only exchange but understanding, and attributed that understanding to cognitive work that binds symbols into meaning (Segments 0900–0906).
This later use extends shared meaning beyond the earlier abstract account without establishing Communication as a separate final theory.


8. Concept lineages became the recording method
After the Context sample, the engineer emphasized that concepts are corrected and rebound over the course of the interaction rather than created as final truth. The agent proposed recording first appearance, later use, drift, correction, present meaning, and open branches, and the engineer said the approach captured what was wanted (Segments 0962–0976).
The exact list and any common frame are agent constructions. The engineer directly supports evolving lineages, not a mandatory multi-part template.

title: Drift
text: Drift names a perceived loss or instability of meaning, terminology, attribution, scope, binding, or alignment. The engineer repeatedly used and corrected the term while working with the agent, and then explicitly rejected its treatment as failure. In the engineer’s account, drift is a useful signal that forward movement should pause because something is not yet sufficiently understood. The step-by-step response to drift presented here is an agent reconstruction, not a method the engineer stated.

title: Drift
text:
Scope
Drift concerns instability in how terms, attributions, contexts, and conceptual relations hold together during the work.
Drift does not itself determine the cause or the remedy. Transcription noise, legitimate contextual rebinding, a missing interface, an unsupported inference, and actual semantic change remain distinct possibilities.

title: Drift
text:
Development through interaction

1. Drift first appeared as a public terminology risk
The engineer described terminology around authoring and authorization as having drifted and required authorship, authoring, authorization, attribution, scope, and delegation to remain distinct before public submission (Segments 0085–0094).
The engineer also identified an unintended language change as drift because terminology moves with language (Segments 0129–0140).


2. Unsupported attribution supplied a live example
When the agent claimed the engineer was noticing a particular boundary, the engineer corrected that claim as the agent’s inference. The agent withdrew the attribution and later agreed to label interpretations (Segments 0504–0521).
The event shows attribution drift and its correction. The label attribution drift is an analytic classification.


3. Contextual crossings became a source of drift
The engineer corrected voice interaction, tool capability, Cadence terminology, and repository terminology as separate contexts, warning that a wrong context would prevent the participants from sharing the same symbol set (Segments 0561–0578).
Later, the engineer identified an unnecessary qualification as a new binding without an interface. The agent named it context leakage through spurious binding (Segments 0611–0620).
The event is engineer-identified; the compact name is the agent’s.


4. Drift was rebound from failure to diagnostic signal
During the inquiry into interfaces and overlap, the agent said the phenomenon was not drift when anchored to foundations. The engineer directly corrected that negative framing: drift is not failure but a useful signal that something is not well defined and that forward movement should stop while the missing understanding is developed (Segments 0673–0681).
The agent then condensed the process into a cycle involving pause, refinement, ontology, binding, and interface. The cycle is derived; the positive signal and the pause requirement are the engineer’s.


5. Overclassification exposed another drift risk
The engineer rejected a detailed software taxonomy because more terminology would create more opportunities for drift and human confusion, and linked the response to simplicity and purpose (Segments 0808–0827).


6. Drift became a rule for revalidating meaning
The engineer later directed that every represented concept be checked against the original exchange that created its meaning, so that correction would not “drift over a drift” (Segment 1019).
This extends Drift from a diagnostic inside the conceptual discussion to a constraint on maintaining what has been derived from it. It does not make the repair infallible; it requires the repair to expose its source and attribution.

title: Conceptual Exploration
text:
Scope
Conceptual Exploration concerns small guesses, marked interpretations, imagined models, and feasibility tests conducted in conversation.
Its boundary is execution. Precision, feasibility, or sustained discussion does not itself authorize a file change, implementation, plan, or effect on another real-world domain. The page does not establish a formal authorization protocol.

title: Conceptual Exploration
text:
Development through interaction

1. Small guesses replaced a full formal proposal
While developing the file-tree architecture, the engineer asked for a small top-level guess rather than a plan or formal proposal. The engineer described the work as an evolving scaffold built one step at a time and warned that producing plans and files around every thought was noisy and lossy (Segments 0580–0584).
The agent’s four-domain guess in Segment 0584 was an exploratory proposal, not a settled architecture.


2. Interpretation was allowed when marked
After correcting an unsupported inference, the engineer said that the agent’s interpretations are valued because they help create symbols and concepts. The engineer required the agent to mark them as interpretations, symmetrically with human interpretation (Segments 0509–0521).
This permits conceptual contribution without transferring its authorship.


3. Exploration became an imagination domain
The engineer corrected an agent response that had brought operational instruction back into a conceptual elaboration. The engineer described changing point of view, creating analogies and hyperboles, reconstructing possible instructions, and mentally modeling feasibility, and contrasted a city imagined in the mind with action affecting real people or domains (Segments 0828–0831).
The agent named a conceptual sandbox for testing feasibility and stated an explore-versus-execute gate. The engineer continued by naming the activity imagination. The sandbox phrase is an agent formulation; the imagination-action distinction is engineer-established.


4. An Erlang sandbox remained deferred
The engineer related the exploration to an earlier Erlang idea for a virtual exchange of messages, concepts, and symbol bindings, said that attempt had not gone well, and said it might be revisited later (Segments 0832–0833).
No present architecture, implementation, or authorization follows from that discussion.


5. The boundary was tested again during extraction
When the agent created a derived document before implementation was authorized, it acknowledged the error. The engineer allowed the result to remain as an example while clarifying that the current exchange was still elaboration (Segments 0934–0937).

title: Authority, Capability, and Delegation
text: The interaction between an engineer and an AI agent exposed five relations that must remain distinct: authority, capability, authorization, scope, and delegation. The engineer establishes intent and retains decision authority. The agent contributes interpretation and uses available capabilities only within an authorized and bounded assignment. The distinction prevents technical access, conversational initiative, or contribution to the work from being mistaken for ownership of the project or its decisions.

title: Authority, Capability, and Delegation
text: The interaction between an engineer and an AI agent exposed five relations that must remain distinct: authority, capability, authorization, scope, and delegation. The engineer establishes intent and retains decision authority. The agent contributes interpretation and uses available capabilities only within an authorized and bounded assignment. The distinction prevents technical access, conversational initiative, or contribution to the work from being mistaken for ownership of the project or its decisions.

title: Authority, Capability, and Delegation
text:
Five distinct relations
The inquiry concerns who decides, what an actor or tool can do, which operation has been authorized, what boundary constrains it, and which work has been assigned to the agent.
Capability does not create authority. Access does not supply authorization. Delegation does not transfer authorship or project ownership. A conversation about a possible action does not itself delegate that action.

title: Authority, Capability, and Delegation
text:
Development through interaction

1. Use of the project-local workspace was confused with control
The engineer asked whether the agent felt comfortable taking control of the former .authoring/ area for its purpose. The agent denied personal intent or ownership and said it could use the directory for authorized work. The engineer corrected the emphasis: decision authority was already established; the active problem was terminology drift around adjacent concepts such as authoring and authorization (Segments 0080–0087).
The agent’s ownership disclaimer did not answer the engineer’s question. The correction reoriented the inquiry toward the relations themselves.


2. Attribution, scope, and delegation were separated
The engineer added that attribution, scope, and delegation also had to be stabilized. The agent proposed keeping attribution about source, scope about boundaries, and delegation about task assignment, without turning assistance into authorship or authority. The engineer adopted this separation as the working frame (Segments 0088–0094).
The exact definitions are agent formulations. The requirement to separate the terms and preserve the frame is engineer-established.


3. Interaction cadence raised an operational-role proposal
The engineer asked for a stronger interaction style while retaining decision authority. The agent proposed taking operational initiative and setting cadence within delegated work while the engineer retained ownership and decisions (Segments 0543–0558).
The complete operational-role formulation remains an agent proposal rather than an adopted statement.


4. Local computer, application, and repository separated capability from authority
The engineer corrected an account that omitted the local operational domain and explained that the agent’s tools permit bounded work on the engineer’s behalf. The agent distinguished capability in local and application layers from authorization supplied by a request, and denied that access creates unrestricted authority (Segments 0559–0563).
The following engineer correction retained the bounded layers while moving voice style, tool capability, Cadence terminology, and repository operations into their respective contexts (Segments 0561–0568).

title: Artifact Maturity and Presentation
text: The interaction between an engineer and an AI agent separated three questions that can otherwise be collapsed: an artifact’s actual maturity, the role it is intended to perform, and how that role is presented to an audience. The distinction was tested through the concept-index case. The agent reported a mock-up maturity state, the engineer established a demonstration purpose, and implementation demonstration case became the accepted working role. The public presentation and the underlying maturity disclosure remain unresolved.

title: Artifact Maturity and Presentation

The public presentation and the underlying maturity disclosure remain unresolved.

title: Artifact Maturity and Presentation
text:
Scope
Artifact Maturity and Presentation concerns the relation among an artifact’s observed state, its intended use, and the claims made about it to an audience.
An intended demonstration role does not establish runtime operation, acceptance-test completion, or deployment. Presentation choices also do not decide those facts. The recorded interaction leaves open how a persuasive submission should distinguish demonstrations, POCs, deployed work, and unverified implementation claims.

title: Artifact Maturity and Presentation
text:
Development through interaction

1. The agent reported a mock-up maturity state
After checking the concept-index application, the agent described it as a documented implementation mock-up whose intended workflow and safeguards were defined while runtime operation and acceptance testing remained pending (Segment 0061).
This was an agent report, not independent verification of the implementation.


2. The engineer established the demonstration purpose
The engineer described the artifact as an extensive, presentable, and robust example of what agentic AI tools can produce (Segment 0062). This established its intended purpose as a demonstration.


3. The agent proposed a maturity-aware label
The agent proposed local implementation mock-up or demonstration case instead of treating the artifact as a deployed system (Segment 0064).
The label was an agent proposal. It did not determine the artifact’s verified maturity.


4. The demonstration role was adopted
The engineer adopted implementation demonstration case as the artifact’s role in the final submission (Segment 0065).
The adoption applies to the role. It does not confirm every maturity statement made by the agent.


5. Presentation and disclosure diverged
The engineer then proposed a marketing-oriented presentation that would not call the artifact a mock-up and would place demonstrations alongside deployed work and POCs. The agent proposed separating those categories so presentation would not blur maturity (Segments 0065–0070).
The engineer deferred that taxonomy and returned to the file-tree inquiry (Segment 0071). No final disclosure rule was adopted.

title: Storage
text:
Scope
Storage concerns files, directories, paths, containment, placement, and the representation of other project concepts in a filesystem tree.
It does not contain every project concept merely because its directories contain artifacts. It is not established as only a physical layer, and a current path does not automatically prove a final conceptual classification.

title: Storage
text:
Development through interaction

1. The active inquiry narrowed to project storage
The engineer asked whether CI-DIGITAL file-tree architecture meant the project context for Storage. The agent answered that Storage was the physical expression rather than the whole project context. The engineer stopped that qualification as leakage outside the active question and restated the immediate boundary as CI-DIGITAL project storage and file-tree domains (Segments 0609–0612).
The correction does not prove that Storage has no relation to physical representation. It shows that the agent’s extra hierarchy was not warranted in that active exchange.


2. Storage and Development became sibling project domains
When the engineer returned to the broader CI-DIGITAL project, the agent mistakenly placed Development under Storage. The engineer corrected the hierarchy: Storage and Development are separate, bounded project domains (Segments 0621–0635).


3. A directory became a contextual representation
The engineer then distinguished Development as a project concept from development/ within Storage, while saying they concern the same thing viewed differently because context changes. The agent called the directory a storage representation and an interface between views (Segments 0634–0638).
The representation insight is the engineer’s; interface and contextual view are agent condensations.


4. Later moves instantiated possible storage views
The engineer reported manually arranging AI/assistant/ and moving the Manifest, docs, and KB beneath Content (Segments 0806–0807 and 0860–0868). These episodes show how conceptual distinctions can be expressed in Storage, but they belong primarily to the AI Assistance and Content lineages.

title: File Tree as Contextual Index
text: A file tree can orient a reader to a domain before any detailed content is opened. The engineer raised this as a problem of domain boundaries, then demonstrated it with the agent by asking it to classify a folder from its path alone. The interaction established that the tree symbolizes denser content and can defer deeper access, while also showing that tree text is not self-validating authority. File Tree as Contextual Index is an analytic label, not a term the engineer adopted.

title: File Tree as Contextual Index
text:
Scope
The concept concerns how directory placement and path sequence provide compact domain orientation before detailed content is opened.
The tree is a representation. It cannot prove that every directory is a semantic domain, that a copied tree is an instruction, or that the represented content is correct.

title: File Tree as Contextual Index
text:
Development through interaction

1. File structure was recognized as carrying boundary information
The engineer opened the restructuring inquiry by saying that file-tree structure brings information about domain boundaries and that earlier local work had made boundary mistakes. The engineer required normalization with preservation rather than removal (Segments 0034–0039).
This establishes the motivating problem. It does not adopt the agent’s early public/work/evidence/private taxonomy.


2. The arranged tree became a reported top-level view
After the engineer reported moving Manifest, docs, and KB beneath Content, the engineer asked the agent to inspect the file architecture as distinctions among domains. The agent reported AI, content, worktree, and root controls as the visible shape (Segments 0860–0873).
That layout is an agent report, not independent verification of the current state or a final architecture decision.


3. UART demonstrated path-based orientation
The engineer asked which domain the UART folder belonged to without opening it. From worktree/hardware/UART, the agent identified a hardware implementation work unit. The engineer confirmed that only the tree had been needed and described the tree as another representation symbolizing the domain (Segments 0874–0886).


4. The representation reduced the cost of deeper access
The engineer said the file structure can represent much denser content and defer opening it until needed. Entering UART then activates the hardware context and its relevant terminology (Segments 0886–0897).
The terms compact, on-demand, and domain scoping were supplied by the agent and welcomed in the flow, but remain agent wording.


5. A copied tree was corrected from authority to example
When the agent treated a tree inserted in a README as authority, the engineer corrected it: the tree had been copied from the conversation as an example of the kind of transposition the engineer wanted. The engineer wanted patterns and provenance analyzed, not instructions inferred from the inserted text (Segments 0919–0937).

title: Simplicity
text: Simplicity concerns how much distinction and structure the current purpose actually requires. The engineer named the concept after rejecting a detailed taxonomy as too much infrastructure and less meaning. Through correction of the agent’s wording, purpose, rather than intent or elaboration, became the relation that tells the work when to stop.

title: Simplicity
text: Simplicity concerns how much distinction and structure the current purpose actually requires. The engineer named the concept after rejecting a detailed taxonomy as too much infrastructure and less meaning. Through correction of the agent’s wording, purpose, rather than intent or elaboration, became the relation that tells the work when to stop.

title: Simplicity
text:
Scope
Simplicity weighs semantic value, classification cost, attention, and navigability against the current purpose.
It does not mean absence of structure, automatic preference for the fewest files, or permission to erase a material boundary. It also does not make every agent efficiency suggestion an adopted principle.

title: Simplicity
text:
Development through interaction

1. Small guesses established a working cadence
The engineer rejected a formal top-level plan in favor of small guesses, one layer at a time, so the conceptual scaffold could evolve without a file or bureaucratic artifact around every thought (Segments 0580–0584).
This supplied the method’s early economy but did not yet name Simplicity.


2. Temporal economy became avoidance of churn
When the agent tried to reverse a premature change, the engineer said to freeze the current state and avoid repeating the same action unnecessarily. The agent proposed churn, and the engineer explicitly adopted that term (Segments 0768–0780).
This relation belongs primarily to Temporal Axis but informs the attention cost of Simplicity.


3. Attention and energy were treated as scarce
The engineer stopped an unnecessary inspection because the answer was already known, and described energy as scarce while many concepts were arriving at once. The agent proposed stopping at each stable distinction, recording it once, and moving on (Segments 0784–0790).
That operationalization is an agent proposal; the engineer’s direct contribution is the scarcity and stopping rationale.


4. Hyperclassification produced confusion
The agent proposed a detailed taxonomy for OpenCode and Codex. The engineer rejected it at the upper level because it was not relevant, created more terminology, and increased drift and human confusion. The engineer summarized the problem as too much infrastructure and less meaning and named the counter-concept Simplicity (Segments 0808–0822).


5. Purpose became the stopping relation
The agent said to stop when the intent was served. The engineer corrected the operative word to purpose, and the agent formulated: stop when the purpose is served, not when the model is most elaborate. The engineer explicitly accepted the relation (Segments 0823–0826).
The sentence form is agent-origin; purpose as the criterion is the engineer’s correction.

O DUT é o módulo uart_controller, organizado em torno de uma interface de registradores e de uma interface UART serial. A verificação foi estruturada no estilo proto-UVM, com BFMs, agentes, monitores, scoreboard e cobertura.

A REGISTER INTERFACE é utilizada para operar o UART CONTROLLER, enquanto a UART INTERFACE representa a terminação física do protocolo serial implementado.
Os principais blocos de design são:

reg_bank
clock_div
tx_uart.sv
rx_uart.sv




Na verificação em estilo UVM/proto-UVM, o repositório utiliza:

dois BFMs, um para cada interface
dois agentes de teste, um para TX e outro para RX
ambiente com monitores, scoreboard e cobertura




No exemplo base disponível no repositório, o caso de teste executa sequências aleatórias e valida a comunicação UART, verificando principalmente se o byte transmitido é igual ao byte recebido.



Partindo do código base disponível no repositório, a evolução natural da verificação consiste em criar novos casos de teste independentes do teste de comunicação byte-a-byte.
Esses novos testes devem avaliar outros aspectos do comportamento do UART, por exemplo:

variação de baud rate
inserção e detecção de erro de paridade
outros efeitos de configuração e status do protocolo




Se erros forem identificados em simulação, eles devem ser analisados a partir de evidências observadas durante a execução.
A análise deve incluir:

características do erro
causa provável
justificativa técnica
estratégia adotada para contornar, corrigir ou explicar o problema




A entrega final deve conter:

o repositório com todos os arquivos relevantes
a implementação realizada
um relatório com observações, evolução do trabalho, detalhamento técnico e análise dos problemas encontrados

A REGISTER INTERFACE é utilizada para operar o UART CONTROLLER, enquanto a UART INTERFACE representa a terminação física do protocolo serial implementado.
Os principais blocos de design são:

reg_bank
clock_div
tx_uart.sv
rx_uart.sv




Na verificação em estilo UVM/proto-UVM, o repositório utiliza:

dois BFMs, um para cada interface
dois agentes de teste, um para TX e outro para RX
ambiente com monitores, scoreboard e cobertura




No exemplo base disponível no repositório, o caso de teste executa sequências aleatórias e valida a comunicação UART, verificando principalmente se o byte transmitido é igual ao byte recebido.



Partindo do código base disponível no repositório, a evolução natural da verificação consiste em criar novos casos de teste independentes do teste de comunicação byte-a-byte.
Esses novos testes devem avaliar outros aspectos do comportamento do UART, por exemplo:

variação de baud rate
inserção e detecção de erro de paridade
outros efeitos de configuração e status do protocolo




Se erros forem identificados em simulação, eles devem ser analisados a partir de evidências observadas durante a execução.
A análise deve incluir:

características do erro
causa provável
justificativa técnica
estratégia adotada para contornar, corrigir ou explicar o problema




A entrega final deve conter:

o repositório com todos os arquivos relevantes
a implementação realizada
um relatório com observações, evolução do trabalho, detalhamento técnico e análise dos problemas encontrados

title: UART Overview
text:
The implementation is organized around five modules and one shared type definition.

uart_controller composes the implementation and connects the external register interface to the UART datapath.
reg_bank stores configuration, exposes register reads and writes, captures status, and generates irq.
clock_div derives clk_tx_out and clk_rx_out from clk and baud_rate.
tx_uart serializes tx_data onto tx.
rx_uart captures serial data from rx into rx_out.
uart_baud_rate_t defines the supported baud-rate labels.

The top-level control path begins at the register interface.

Configuration written into reg_bank drives reg_reset, parity_enable, parity_type, stop_bit, data_len, and baud_rate.
baud_rate drives clock_div.
clock_div produces clk_uart_tx and clk_uart_rx for tx_uart and rx_uart.
tx_uart returns tx_done and tx_err to reg_bank.
rx_uart returns data_rx, rx_done, and rx_error to reg_bank.

The top-level data path is split into a transmit path and a receive path.

Transmit path: register write to address 1 -> reg1_data_tx -> data_tx -> tx_uart -> txd
Receive path: rxd -> rx_uart -> data_rx -> reg2_data_rx -> register read at address 2

reg0_config is the central configuration and status register.

Bits 11:0 hold writable configuration fields.
Bits 15:12 are written by the implementation to reflect status.

Observed behavior recorded in device terms:

In the observed transmit scenario with tx_data = 8'hA5, length = 8, parity disabled, and one stop bit, tx produced a start bit, 8 data bits in least-significant-bit first order, and one stop bit.
In the observed receive scenario with an 8-bit frame carrying 8'hA5, parity disabled, and one stop bit, rx_out became 8'hA5 and rx_done asserted at frame completion.
In the observed register scenario, a read of address 2 returned the captured receive byte.

Source-comment intent appears mainly in uart_controller, reg_bank, and clock_div.

uart_controller comments describe the file as the integration point for the register bank, clock divider, receiver, and transmitter.
reg_bank comments describe register ownership, field mapping, and baud-rate conversion.
clock_div comments describe clk_tx_out as a 1x baud-rate clock and clk_rx_out as a 16x baud-rate clock.

title: Data Flow
text:
A register write to address 1 loads reg1_data_tx.
The same write asserts tx_start.
data_tx reflects reg1_data_tx.
tx_uart reads data_tx and emits a UART frame on txd.
tx_done returns to reg_bank.
ready_to_transmit_tx is updated from transmit activity.

title: Data Flow
text:
A register write to address 1 loads reg1_data_tx.
The same write asserts tx_start.
data_tx reflects reg1_data_tx.
tx_uart reads data_tx and emits a UART frame on txd.
tx_done returns to reg_bank.
ready_to_transmit_tx is updated from transmit activity.

title: Data Flow
text:
Receive Flow

rxd enters rx_uart.
rx_uart samples serial data using clk_uart_rx.
rx_uart writes the recovered byte to data_rx.
rx_done returns to reg_bank.
On rx_done_rise, reg2_data_rx captures data_rx.
A register read at address 2 returns reg2_data_rx.

title: Data Flow
text:
Configuration Flow

A register write to address 0 updates reg0_config[11:0].
reg_bank maps reg0_config fields to: reg_reset, parity_enable, parity_type, stop_bit, data_len, and baud_rate.
baud_rate drives clock_div.
clock_div drives clk_uart_tx and clk_uart_rx.
tx_uart and rx_uart consume the configuration signals.

title: Data Flow
text:
Status Flow

rx_error, tx_error, data_available_rx, and ready_to_transmit_tx are mirrored into reg0_config[15:12].
data_available_flag and ready_to_transmit_flag contribute to irq.
irq is exported through uart_controller.

title: Data Flow
text:
Observed Behavior

In the observed transmit scenario, the transmit path carried 8'hA5 from the transmit data register to the serial output.
In the observed receive scenario, the receive path carried 8'hA5 from the serial input to rx_out, and a register read returned the captured receive byte in the register path.

title: Register Map
text: The implementation exposes a 2-bit address field.

title: Register Map
text:
Address 0
Register name:

reg0_config

Read behavior:

data_out = {16'd0, reg0_config}

Write behavior:

reg0_config[11:0] <= data_in[11:0]

Fields:

bit 0: reg_reset
bit 1: parity_enable
bit 2: parity_type
bit 3: stop_bit
bits 6:4: data-length code
bits 11:7: baud-rate code
bit 12: data_available_rx
bit 13: ready_to_transmit_tx
bit 14: rx_error
bit 15: tx_error

Notes:

bits 15:12 are written by the implementation as status mirrors
data_len is formed as reg0_config[6:4] + 1

title: Register Map
text:
Address 1
Register name:

reg1_data_tx

Write behavior:

reg1_data_tx <= data_in[7:0]
tx_start <= '1

Read behavior:

no read path is implemented for address 1

title: Register Map
text:
Address 2
Register name:

reg2_data_rx

Read behavior:

data_out = {24'd0, reg2_data_rx}
data_available_rx <= '0

Write behavior:

no write path is implemented for address 2

Update source:

reg2_data_rx <= data_rx on rx_done_rise

title: Register Map
text:
Default Read Behavior

data_out <= 32'd0

Observed Behavior

A write to address 1 loads the transmit byte and asserts tx_start.
A read of address 2 returns the captured receive byte.

title: clock_div
text:
Divider Structure
CNT_WIDTH is defined as:
$clog2((CLK_FREQ / 50) / 2)
max_count is selected by baud_rate.

For clk_tx_out, the terminal count source is max_count.
For clk_rx_out, the terminal count source is max_count >> 4.

On rst:

counter_tx <= '0
counter_rx <= '0
clk_tx_out <= 0
clk_rx_out <= 0
max_count_tx_reg <= '0
max_count_rx_reg <= '0

During operation:

max_count_tx_reg stores max_count
max_count_rx_reg stores max_count >> 4
each output toggles when its counter reaches the stored terminal count

title: Making a UART failure tell a clearer story
text:
A first example from AI-Pipeline Tools for VLSI Workflows.
A UART test sends a byte. The receiver returns a different one. The simulation log records the mismatch, while a separate waveform records what happened inside the design. Explaining the failure means bringing those two views together.
That small gap in a custom workflow is where this C++ helper belongs. It connects a reported failure to the corresponding signal values, producing a compact, readable account that can become part of a technical report or a classroom explanation.
crumbs: Making a UART failure tell a clearer story

title: Making a UART failure tell a clearer story
text:
One question, two sources
The question is concrete: what did the signals show when the test reported the wrong byte?
vcd_snapshot.cpp reads a saved simulation log and a VCD file—the text format used here to record waveform changes. It takes the timestamp, expected byte, and received byte from a selected mismatch in the log. It then finds the requested signals in the waveform and prints their values alongside that failure.
The detail that makes this useful is temporal: a waveform stores changes, so a signal may have acquired its value before the failure was reported. The helper follows each selected signal to its latest recorded change at or before the requested time. Its built-in UART signal groups bring the configuration, serial interface, receive logic, and receive register into the same account.





flowchart LR
    L[Saved simulation log] -->|Failure time and bytes| H[C++ snapshot helper]
    W[Saved waveform from the same run] -->|Selected signal values| H
    H --> R[Compact correlation report]
    R --> D[Explanation in the technical document]
crumbs: Making a UART failure tell a clearer story

title: Making a UART failure tell a clearer story
text:

The correlation process uses this exact event as its worked example. Its companion waveform guide identifies the signals that show the transmitted byte, the receiver’s output, and the stored receive value.
Together, these conclusions give the failure a form an audience can follow: a selected configuration, an expected result, a different observed result, and the internal state associated with that moment. The results report describes the boundary exposed by the test. A snapshot helps examine that result; the timing sequence still matters when explaining its cause.

section: How the tool took shape with AI
text:
How the tool took shape with AI
The archived development conversation from April 22, 2026 records the choices behind the helper. The first requirement was to connect the scoreboard’s expected data with waveform state at a timestamp. The second was that it run standalone, so that someone reviewing the submission would not need the Task runner.
An initial Python approach prompted a discussion of implementation options. A compiled binary was preferred; C and C++ were compared, and light OOP in a single executable was selected. AI assistance turned those choices into source and refined it against the saved example. The development record preserves two practical corrections: accepting the spacing used in waveform signal names and selecting an actual mismatch instead of an earlier successful comparison.
The subsequent recorded run brings the two sources together: the report shows expected 0x37, observed 0x9b, and 0x9b in both the receiver output and stored receive data at the selected timestamp. This is the historical outcome behind the example above.

title: Making a UART failure tell a clearer story
text:
How the work becomes documentation
The comments are written in ordinary language and explain the intent, approach, and small OOP structure. The source’s opening explanation and component comments carry the reasoning behind the arrangement alongside the code that realizes it.
The executable contributes a formatted report of the timestamp, mismatch, and selected signal values. A later request for documentation and help led to the process guide explaining how to use that output in the submission. AI participation spans implementation, refinement, explanation, and preparation of material another person can understand.
The outcome is a small, independent example of AI helping create a useful process inside VLSI verification work. Its contribution to the wider line is easy to recognize: an engineering question becomes a focused tool, and the tool’s output helps make the work explainable.


Source and scope notes


C++ implementation: standalone source for extracting a matching scoreboard entry, resolving signal names, reconstructing values, and printing the report. It also accepts an explicit timestamp and individually selected signals.
Saved VCD waveform: the waveform associated with the boundary example; its declared timescale is 1ps.
Development history: archived OpenCode session SD242 - ATIVIDADE FINAL, April 22, 2026, session ID ses_24cc09407ffeakvUlbgrh9oT6q. Initial C++ creation: prt_db418c6b80013NbWMqWb8A25m8; corrected example output: prt_db41b49f9001ci5SW1bCo6nGvu; explanatory comments: prt_db41bdaec001SAlWFBTBFYTUOu; process documentation update: prt_db41fa2a5001DRWbu4d3wu76pI. These are recovered historical records, read during repository curation.
The helper expects the scoreboard mismatch wording represented in this example. It uses the log timestamp directly, so the log and waveform must refer to the same run and use compatible time units.
The case presents the existing UART outcome and an account of using the helper. It does not establish the mismatch’s root cause or a general result for other UART implementations.

title: Local language tooling: capabilities and boundaries
text:
This note records the language-oriented tools observed on the current CI-DIGITAL workstation. It distinguishes what each kind of tool does, where the capability lives, whether it can be used without VS Code, and what has actually been verified.
The inventory is a local snapshot from September 13, 2026. It is not a claim that every installed component is active in every editor session, and it is not an upstream maintenance assessment. No software was installed while producing this inventory.
